Timing relationship of AVI64 DC events
DC events are fully synchronized to digital pattern but processing of the event data
causes some delay times.
The following basic characteristics are to be considered for programming AVI64 DC
events:
A DC event requires always 32 vectors.
Programming of overlapping DC events is not supported.
Setup commands like the force value, the clamp value, or the forcing mode are
always sent first in the 32 vector block.
Measure commands are always sent last in the 32 vector block.
Processing of the DC events in the front-end adds an additional delay time.
The availability of the measured values depends on the sample mode (coherent or
non-coherent) and the programmed averaging. A measure event defines only the
trigger of the measurement.
Dummy vectors may be required at the end of a pattern to ensure that the
communication between the test processor and the front-end is running until
sampling, data processing, and the data transfer has been finished for the last
measure event.
The following table shows the delay time that is caused by the data transfer to the front-
end and by synchronization to the free running sample clock and the internal clock of
the digital control loop. The table shows the delay of DC events with respect to the
begin of the first event vector in the pattern. The table defines the delay time where the
receiving device like a DAC or ADC of the front-end receives the trigger for changing the
output value or starting sampling. The analog settling time is not covered.

Function Delay time
Set voltage or current (Force or clamp) 8 vectors + (0.1 ... 1.11) µs
Set force mode (Voltage or current) 8 vectors + (0.1 ... 1.11) µs
Set range 8 vectors + (0.1 ... 1.11) µs
High-speed voltage AWG, set voltage 41 vectors
High-resolution voltage AWG, set voltage 9 vectors + 1.5 µs / vector period
Sampling non-coherent 32 vectors + (-0.9 ... 0.11) µs
Sampling coherent 47 vectors

The delay time is referenced to the begin of the first vector of the DC event (T0 in

Non-coherent sampling utilizes the measured values that are already available for

Coherent sampling requires some more vectors for setting up the ADC.

Application note
DC events in reused pattern
For a minimized test time we recommend, not to reuse pattern with DC events that
are to be applied for different AVI64 units or ranges. The recommendation applies to
pattern that are manually created using the related test method APIs but not to the
automatically created SmartRDI pattern.
The AVI64 channels feature several units like the PMU, the floating differential
voltmeter, the floating high-current unit and the high-resolution voltage AWG that
are programmed by the same DC events but require different settings. The pattern
data of related DC events must be reloaded in case the containing pattern is reused
for another unit or a range has changed. This may significantly increase the test time.
The recommendation applies to all DC events that change the force- or clamp value
or range or the measurement range for the following units:
The PMU in normal PMU operating mode with active closed loop control
The PMU in high-speed AWG mode (with disabled closed loop control)
The floating differential voltmeter
The floating high-current unit
The high-resolution voltage AWG
Examples
The following examples demonstrate how to set up an AVI64 pin for a standard current
measurement using the AVI64 Force only connection connection scheme. The code is
applicable also for the other connection schemes AVI64 Kelvin connection, AVI64 reverse
Kelvin connection, and AVI64 Sense only connection, however the specific limitations
must be considered as defined in sections "Limitations of the connection scheme" of the
related topics.
The three examples are set up in a three-step sequence of connecting the pin and
applying the basic setup, measuring the requested parameter, and disconnecting in a
separate task. This sequence is suitable for AVI64-specific tests, since very often more
than one setup has to be applied and more than one measurement has to be carried
out before the pin is disconnected again.
These examples are available in the following sections:
Example 1: SmartRDI, pattern‑based programming
Pattern‑based programming using SmartRDI is the recommended solution that
requires the least amount of code and on the other hand delivers the most stable
result in terms of timing.

Example 2: SmartRDI, code‑based programming
Code‑based programming using SmartRDI needs some more code and must follow
the structure of the wrapped test method APIs.
Example 3: Test method API SPMU_TASK
This example is based on the test method APIs and is strongly tied to the structure
of the underlying commands.
The code of the three examples generates the same measurement sequence for the
programmed pin. If you use the Trace Function to compare the code‑based SmartRDI
example and the example based on the test method APIs, you will get the same output
in the MCDLog file.
Example 1: SmartRDI, pattern‑based programming
The example uses a code‑based RDI command to setup and connect the AVI64 pin. The
following RDI block performs a pattern‑based measurement. The last RDI command
disconnects the AVI64 pin in code‑based mode.
Since the RDI block uses a specialized DC event to perform the measurement, only the
measurement related parameters must be defined. In contrast, for code‑based
programming with SmartRDI or programming with test method APIs, all parameters
must be specified also for the measurement.

AVI64 programming - Kelvin test unit /
sense connection test
The AVI64 card features a Kelvin test unit (or sense-connection test unit), which can be
used to verify that the force lines and sense lines are connected together on the DUT
board or at the DUT pins. The Kelvin test unit is available per channel.
Basic data
Basic data of the AVI64 Kelvin test unit:
The Kelvin test unit is available per channel.
The threshold for the pass/fail decision is about 5 kΩ.
The test current is about 100 µA.
The maximum capacitance between the force lines and the corresponding sense
lines is 5 nF.
The set up and set down of the test is performed in parallel on all selected pins.
Three measurements are serially performed for the P# pin, the PS# pin and the GS#
pin.
Testing eight AVI64 pins requires a test time of about 10 ms per site.
The test can be performed only in the disconnected state of the selected pins.
Topic 148869

API overview
Two APIs support a parallel go/no-go Kelvin test on all active sites and pins and a
detailed Kelvin test on the site in focus. Both APIs perform three measurements for the
three lines P#, PS# and GS# as shown in the diagrams below.
Function checkKelvinStatusParallel()
The function checkKelvinStatusParallel() of class HW_STATE initiates a sense
connection test on the defined pins to verify that the force lines and sense lines are
connected together on the DUT board or at the DUT pins. The test is performed in
parallel for all active sites. The function returns a go/no-go result for each
configured site in a single integer array.
The go/no-go result of the function is set to 0 (Kelvin test has failed) if any of
the tested pins has returned a failing result for any of the three measurements
shown below.
The go/no-go result of the function is set to 1 (Kelvin test has passed) if all
tested pins have successfully finished all three measurements on all active sites.
Function HW_STATE.checkKelvinStatus()
The function initiates a sense connection test for the site in focus. The function
returns individual results for all tested pins in two integer arrays for the positive and
for the negative line:
The measurements for P# and PS# that are shown below are combined into a
single result that is returned in array statusPos. The returned value will be set
to 1 (Kelvin test has passed) only if both the measurement via the P# line and
the measurement via the PS# line have shown a passing result.
The measurement result for the GS# line is returned in array statusNeg.
For ganged pins, the Kelvin test / sense connection test is performed for each individual
channel.

Application notes
Kelvin connection test in a testflow
A continuity test, which is normally performed at the beginning of a testflow, may
use AVI64 channels. The continuity test will show a reliable result only if both the
force and sense pins of the AVI64 channels are connected properly. Therefore, we
recommend implementing a Kelvin test at the beginning of a testflow before the
continuity test is performed.
Reverse Kelvin connection and the Kelvin test unit
When using the Kelvin test unit in combination with the reverse Kelvin connection,
the recommended P# series resistance of 5 kΩ will cause a failing result.
The Kelvin test must be replaced by two separate continuity tests via the P# pogo
pin and via the PS# pogo pin. The connection states "FORCE_ONLY" and
"SENSE_ONLY" are to be used for this purpose. For more information, refer to PMU
operating mode.

Topic 148788

Measurement filters
AVI64 channels feature programmable anti-aliasing, low-pass measurement filters for all
ADCs:
Voltage measurement ADC and current measurement ADC of the PMU
Voltage measurement ADC and current measurement ADC of the floating high-
current unit
Voltage measurement ADC of the floating differential voltmeter
Measurement filter characteristics
Minimum cutoff frequency: 10 Hz
Maximum cutoff frequency: 250 kHz
Default cutoff frequency: 250 kHz
The dynamic behavior of the force output is independent of the measurement filters.

Averaging
All channels of the card feature hardware based averaging of measurements. The
average of multiple consecutive ADC samples is calculated and stored on
board.Hardware based averaging can be utilized for code‑based and pattern‑based
measurements.
Programmable range of samples: 1 ... 65535 (any value supported)
ADC sample frequency: 1 MHz
Some hints to consider:
The sample time for averaged measurements must be taken into account.
Pattern‑based measurements require a minimum number of vectors after the
trigger has been initiated. For more information, refer to Timing of DC events and
the related sub-topics.
The effective maximum sample frequency is the ADC sample frequency of 1 MHz
divided by the number of averaged samples.
The "measurement filter" may be used instead of averaging if a high effective
sample frequency is required. This filter behaves like a simple RC filter. The settling
time is to be considered but the filter setting has no effect on the effective
maximum sample frequency.
The dynamic behavior of the force output is independent of the settings for
averaging.
Averaging cannot be used in combination with the pattern synchronized, high
impedance voltage sampling mode (VM_HIZ_COH) of the PMU: The channel controller
ignores the programmed average value if VM_HIZ_COH measurement mode is selected.

Automatic down-ranging
AVI64 channels feature automatic down-ranging for current measurements.
Automatic down-ranging means that the current range is automatically changed to the
best fit range for the measurement and restored to the original range after the
measurement.
Two parameters define whether the automatic down-ranging is performed or not:
1. The force / clamp current range:
Can be set explicitly or (if not defined)
is automatically derived from the forced or clamped value.
2. The current measurement range:
Can be set explicitly or (if not defined)
is automatically derived from the pass/fail thresholds.
Automatic down-ranging is performed only if the current measurement range is lower
than the force / clamp current range regardless whether the ranges have been set
explicitly or have been selected automatically.
With automatic down‑ranging active, the next lower current range is activated only if
the measured current does not exceed 90 % of the next lower current range.
Automatic down-ranging is supported for both code‑based programming using the
SPMU_TASK and DPS_TASK test method APIs and the pattern‑based programming using
the DC events and is also supported by SmartRDI.

Application notes
Flush vectors at the end of a pattern
Due to inter module communication it is required to keep the pattern running for a
short time after the last ADC measurement related DC event. The actual required
time or number of flush vectors depends on the setup. In case of insufficient number
of vectors before pattern stop, a communication error might occur and
measurement results might be lost.
The number of required flush vectors depends on the average count and the pattern
cycle time as follows:
PMU, differential voltmeter and floating high-current unit:
Minimum number of vectors = 45 + ( (average + 1) / (1 MHz * period) )
PMU in pattern synchronized measurement mode ("VM_HIZ_COH"):
Minimum number of vectors = 37 + (average / (1 MHz * period) )
where: average = Programmed average count
period = Cycle time of the pattern
The calculated number is the minimum number of vectors that is required between
the last measure event and the end of the pattern.
The minimum number of vectors may be higher if TMU measurements are started in
the same pattern as the ADC measurements.
Note that the TSST? - (TeSt STatus) firmware command can be used to check for
missing samples: Bit 8 is set if a measurement is lost.
Measure filter settling time
The programmable digital low-pass measure filters for all ADCs behave like simple
RC filters. A short settling time is to be applied or some samples are to be ignored to
settle to an acceptable difference to the input signal.
Two operating modes are to be considered for estimating the required settling time
or number of samples:
Normal operating mode of the digital closed loop control
The continuous trigger for the ADCs is defined by the 1 MHz operating
frequency of the digital closed loop control. This mode is utilized for all
measurement modes except the coherent voltage sampling mode. The settling
time of the measure filter has to be considered in this mode.
Coherent voltage sampling mode

The trigger for the ADCs is defined only by DC measure events in a pattern. A
minimum number of samples as defined in the following formulas and examples
has to be considered in this mode.

Averaging
All channels of the card feature hardware based averaging of measurements. The
average of multiple consecutive ADC samples is calculated and stored on
board.Hardware based averaging can be utilized for code‑based and pattern‑based
measurements.
Programmable range of samples: 1 ... 65535 (any value supported)
ADC sample frequency: 1 MHz
Some hints to consider:
The sample time for averaged measurements must be taken into account.
Pattern‑based measurements require a minimum number of vectors after the
trigger has been initiated. For more information, refer to Timing of DC events and
the related sub-topics.
The effective maximum sample frequency is the ADC sample frequency of 1 MHz
divided by the number of averaged samples.
The "measurement filter" may be used instead of averaging if a high effective
sample frequency is required. This filter behaves like a simple RC filter. The settling
time is to be considered but the filter setting has no effect on the effective
maximum sample frequency.
The dynamic behavior of the force output is independent of the settings for
averaging.
Averaging cannot be used in combination with the pattern synchronized, high
impedance voltage sampling mode (VM_HIZ_COH) of the PMU: The channel controller
ignores the programmed average value if VM_HIZ_COH measurement mode is selected.

Flush vectors at the end of a pattern
Due to inter module communication it is required to keep the pattern running for a
short time after the last ADC measurement related DC event. The actual required
time or number of flush vectors depends on the setup. In case of insufficient number
of vectors before pattern stop, a communication error might occur and
measurement results might be lost.
The number of required flush vectors depends on the average count and the pattern
cycle time as follows:
PMU, differential voltmeter and floating high-current unit:
Minimum number of vectors = 45 + ( (average + 1) / (1 MHz * period) )
PMU in pattern synchronized measurement mode ("VM_HIZ_COH"):
Minimum number of vectors = 37 + (average / (1 MHz * period) )
where: average = Programmed average count
period = Cycle time of the pattern
The calculated number is the minimum number of vectors that is required between
the last measure event and the end of the pattern.
The minimum number of vectors may be higher if TMU measurements are started in
the same pattern as the ADC measurements.
Note that the TSST? - (TeSt STatus) firmware command can be used to check for
missing samples: Bit 8 is set if a measurement is lost.
Measure filter settling time
The programmable digital low-pass measure filters for all ADCs behave like simple
RC filters. A short settling time is to be applied or some samples are to be ignored to
settle to an acceptable difference to the input signal.
Two operating modes are to be considered for estimating the required settling time
or number of samples:
Normal operating mode of the digital closed loop control
The continuous trigger for the ADCs is defined by the 1 MHz operating
frequency of the digital closed loop control. This mode is utilized for all
measurement modes except the coherent voltage sampling mode. The settling
time of the measure filter has to be considered in this mode.
Coherent voltage sampling mode

The trigger for the ADCs is defined only by DC measure events in a pattern. A
minimum number of samples as defined in the following formulas and examples
has to be considered in this mode.
The required settling time of the filter or the number of samples to be ignored
depends on the accepted maximum relative error and the effective filter frequency
and is calculated as follows:
Settling time = -1.0 * ln (Maximum relative error) / (2 * π * Filter frequency)
Number of samples = Settling time * Sample frequency
where: Maximum relative error = Maximum accepted relative error at the end of the settling time
Filter frequency = Effective filter frequency
Sample frequency = ADC sample frequency
ln = Natural logarithm

Application notes
Current surge tracker and current measurement range
The surge tracker in current sensing mode uses the current measurement values of
the digital control loop as input:
The effective maximum and minimum thresholds are limited by the actual
current measurement range.
SmarTest supports programming the thresholds to values outside of the actual
current measurement range.
Therefore, the same thresholds can be maintained over a complete test suite or
testflow but the effective thresholds are always truncated to the actual current
measurement range.
Example:
1. High current threshold of the surge tracker set to 100 mA.
2. Current range set to 200 mA: The surge tracker will detect current spikes higher
than 100 mA.
3. Current range changed to 50 mA: The thresholds of the surge tracker are
truncated to ±50 mA.
4. A current spike higher than 50 mA will trigger the current surge tracker
although the high threshold is still set to 100 mA.
Note: For fast load changes and the example above, the maximum current of an
AVI64 channel in the 50 mA range will be clamped to 75 mA (typical) by the Fast
clamp current functionality.
TMU and surge tracker
The TMU (Time measurement unit) and the surge tracker cannot be used in parallel.
The two functionalities use the same comparators that can be assigned to only one
of them at the same time.
Surge tracker is silently disabled in temporarily unganged mode
Note that on AVI64, DPS128/64, and FVI16 you cannot execute a current compare on
a ganged group of channels if the group is in unganged mode. Already activated
comparators are silently disabled in unganged mode. A user notification (Error or
warning) is omitted in this case, to avoid any interrupt in the testflow. The previous
state of the comparators is automatically restored after the ganged group has been
restored.
Surge tracker monitors either voltage or current but not both

Although the digital closed loop control of AVI64 channels samples voltage and
current simultaneously, the surge tracker can monitor either the voltage or the
current but not both at the same time.

AVI64 channel operating mode and TMU

TMU and API "waitTMUFinished"

The AVI64 TMU is optimized for single shot measurements. The front end will

The time measurement unit (TMU) of an AVI64 channel in PMU operating mode is
programmed by test method APIs and SmartRDI functions. DC events are used for
sequencer controlled setup and arming of the TMU.
Topic 346895

TMU characteristics
The following items must be considered when using the TMU:
The TMU is supported in the PMU operating mode and in the Digital I/O operating
mode.
The TMU is not supported in the DPS operating mode.
For ganged pins, the time measurement unit (TMU) is supported but only the
high‑speed voltage comparator and the high‑resolution voltage comparator of the
PMU can be used. The measurement is performed on the master channel. The
high‑resolution current comparator of the PMU and the comparators of the shared
resources are not supported.
The default connection set must be used for TMU measurements.
The TMU uses features that are designed for digital pins. Therefore, the DC Scale
specific connection sets cannot be used. TMU measurements can be applied only
on pins defined in the default connection set.
For more information regarding the default connection set refer to Digital Pins
editor and DFPN, DFPN?.
Basic considerations for programming TMU measurements
The following items should be considered for TMU measurements both using SmartRDI
or TM APIs:
The arm event is the reference for the time stamps.
The arm event is automatically inserted into the pattern burst by SmartRDI and
must be manually inserted for programming by TM API using EVENT_TMU_START.
Time stamps are recorded only after a TMU measure event has been executed in
the pattern.
A measure event is inserted into the pattern by SmartRDI function
rdi.tmu().measMode() or by TM API EVENT_TMU_MEAS.
The basic comparator settings must be applied before the pattern or pattern burst
is started.
Although the related SmartRDI functions can be programmed only in pattern‑based
mode, SmartRDI applies the settings before the pattern burst is started.
For test method API based programming, the related settings must be applied by
the DPS_AUX_PIN_TASK API as shown below.

Measurement filters
AVI64 channels feature programmable anti-aliasing, low-pass measurement filters for all
ADCs:
Voltage measurement ADC and current measurement ADC of the PMU
Voltage measurement ADC and current measurement ADC of the floating high-
current unit
Voltage measurement ADC of the floating differential voltmeter
Measurement filter characteristics
Minimum cutoff frequency: 10 Hz
Maximum cutoff frequency: 250 kHz
Default cutoff frequency: 250 kHz
The dynamic behavior of the force output is independent of the measurement filters.
Note  The high-resolution comparators of the TMU utilize the continuous data
stream of the ADCs. The measurement filter setting has therefore also an effect on
the TMU measurements.
For high-speed TMU measurements using the high-resolution comparators, we
therefore recommend setting the measurement filter to the maximum value.

SmartRDI overview
The complete TMU functionality is covered by the tmu() API of SmartRDI. For more
information refer to SmartRDI: TMU test setup and the related member functions of the
API.
The TMU core functionality is supported only in the pattern‑based mode of SmartRDI.
The code‑based mode is not supported. We strongly recommend using the
pattern‑based mode with the execution mode set to TA::BURST or TA::PROD. The
mode TA::SINGLE is not recommended for TMU measurements. For more information
refer to RDI_BEGIN().

Application notes
TMU and surge tracker
The TMU (Time measurement unit) and the surge tracker cannot be used in parallel.
The two functionalities use the same comparators that can be assigned to only one
of them at the same time.
Dummy vectors between EVENT_TMU_MEAS and the edge to be measured
Some dummy vectors are required to set up and activate the measurement unit. A
delay time of minimum 100 ns is required between the EVENT_TMU_MEAS and the
first comparator event to be recorded. Comparator events are not recorded and will
be lost if these vectors are omitted.
Number of vectors before pattern end
Due to inter module communication it is required to keep the pattern running for a
short time after the last TMU related DC event. The actual required time depends on
the setup. In case of insufficient number of vectors before pattern stop, a
communication error might occur.
Rules:
Do not specify less than 41 vectors.
60 vectors should work for most of the applications.
If the test execution stops with a communication error, add additional vectors at the
end of the pattern to ensure the error is not caused by an insufficient number of
vectors.
The TMU and the DC event controlled measurements utilize the same path to
transfer data from the front end to the test processor. The combination of the two
kinds of measurements in the same pattern burst on the same pin may increase the
required number of vectors before the pattern end.
TMU and API "waitTMUFinished"
Executing API TMU_PINS.waitTMUfinished() after running the TMU measurement
pattern is mandatory but you cannot rely on the returned status information. The API
TMU_RESULTS.getNumberOfMeasuredSamples() is to be used for checking the
number of valid samples.
The AVI64 TMU is optimized for single shot measurements. The front end will
automatically append eight dummy samples at the end of a measurement to enable
the TMU handling single shot measurements. The dummy samples cannot be
uploaded but are taken into account by API TMU_PINS.waitTMUfinished().
Missing samples

The AVI64 TMU is able to handle up to eight missing samples. If the sample count,
programmed by API TMU_PINS.setNumSamples(), cannot be acquired, the following
behavior will be observed:
1 … 8 samples missing: The captured values can be uploaded.
More than eight samples missing: No values can be uploaded. The API
TMU_RESULTS.getNumberOfMeasuredSamples() will return 0 for the respective
pin and all measurements.
High-resolution current comparators are silently disabled in temporarily unganged
mode
Note that on AVI64, DPS128/64, and FVI16 you cannot execute a current compare on
a ganged group of channels if the group is in unganged mode. Already activated
comparators are silently disabled in unganged mode. A user notification (Error or
warning) is omitted in this case, to avoid any interrupt in the testflow. The previous
state of the comparators is automatically restored after the ganged group has been
restored.

AVI64 Use Case - SmartRDI - Differential
voltmeter (DiffVM)
The DiffVM is available per eight AVI64 channel group. The DiffVM can be connected to
any combination of two AVI64 channels of the same eight pin group or to a single AVI64
channel and the common GND. For the assignment of the channel groups refer to AVI64
channel group and differential compare assignment.
The DiffVM takes over the voltage measure functionality floating high-current unit
(HCU) and therefore the DiffVM cannot be used separately if the HCU of the same eight
channel group is connected.
The DiffVM can be used to measure voltage on a passive pin, or to measure voltage
between active pins. In that case the voltage feedback for the digital closed loop control
of the active pins is still based on the per-channel voltmeter, but the measurement is
done by the DiffVM.
As soon as rdi.dc().refPin() is programmed and set to any other pin of the same eight pin
group, the DiffVM will be used for the voltage measurements.

AVI64 Use Case - SmartRDI - High-current
unit (HCU)
The HCU is a floating high current unit, which has one current range (4A). For voltage
measurement it occupies the DiffVM. HCU and DiffVM are available per group of eight
channels.
The positive output (#HF + #HS) of the source is the pin which owns the HCU
(programmed pin). The HCU is selected by the function rdi.dc().mode(TA::HiCurrent).
The negative output (#LF + #LS) is either another AVI64 channel (from the same eight
pin group) or GND. GND can be programmed, using rdi.dc().refPin(TA::GND).
Because it is a floating power source, that can be connected to active DUT-pins (whit
unknown conditions) it is a good practice to use rdi.dc().preCharge(TA::SAFE_CON) for
spike free connection.
The Unit has no continuous current capability. The floating energy storage of the unit is
only charged, if the unit is not connected, therefore if you want to be sure that the
generated signal had sufficient power, check the provided charge status flags or
measure both current and voltage. See AVI64 Use Case - SmartRDI - HCU flags for an
example on how to check the flags.

HCU current clamp
If the HCU is used in voltage mode, the current clamp cannot be programmed lower
than 2 % of the current range (symmetrical clamp lower than 80 mA). If lower values are
needed, the current clamp has to be programmed asymmetrically, for example,
rdi.dc().iClamp(-20 mA, 200 mA), otherwise the HW-forced clamp can be different from
the programmed. This behavior is to avoid oscillating of the hardware and is not yet
covered by the Software.

AVI64 Use Case - SmartRDI - HCU stacked
It is possible to stack the HCU; however, it must be done manually. There is no SW
model to support it.
Any two (or more) HCUs may be stacked. To stack HCUs, a common connection point
must be established between each pair of stacked HCUs (see star point between CH02
& CH09 in setup diagram). Two stacked HCUs are able to deliver up to 16V at 4A.
CAUTION The floating range of the HCU is -30 V ... +80. The voltage at either of
the force and sense pins must not exceed floating range. This applies to all pins of
all stacked HCUs.

AVI64 Use Case - SmartRDI - PMU AWG/DGT
An AVI64 PMU can be utilized as arbitrary waveform generator (AWG) or as digitizer
(DGT). Both functionalities are supported for voltage and current.
The AWG/DGT functionality is achieved by DC events in digital pattern. The basic setup
and the connections are to be done by the same APIs that are used for the static setup
of the PMU.
PMU AWG
The PMU AWG supports a normal operating mode and a high-speed operating mode:
PMU AWG in default operating mode
The PMU operating mode supports the AWG for all measurement modes. The
digital closed loop control is enabled in this mode. Force and measure events are
defined by the pattern but a delay of up to 1 µs for synchronizing to the free
running 1 MHz clock of the control loop is to be taken into account.
PMU AWG in high-speed voltage mode
The digital closed loop control is disabled for this mode and the DUT is connected
only via the force pin P# or via the sense pin PS#. The timing behavior depends
strictly on the pattern clock. The maximum sampling rate in this mode is 3 Msps
(million samples per second).
This AWG mode supports forcing voltages with a fixed clamp current that
corresponds to the maximum current of the force voltage range. Measuring
voltages and currents is also supported in this AWG mode but a jitter of up to 1 µs
for synchronizing to the free running 1 MHz sample clock is to be considered. For
more information refer to AVI64 Use Case - SmartRDI - PMU in high-speed AWG
mode.

PMU DGT
The PMU DGT supports a normal operating mode and coherent voltage sampling mode:
PMU DGT in default operating mode
The measured values are derived from the already sampled values of the digital
closed loop control that operates with a free running 1 MHz clock. A jitter up to
about 1 µs is to be considered for an average count of one sample. Additional
sampling time is to be taken into account for an average count of more than one
sample.
PMU DGT in coherent voltage sampling mode
The PMU features an additional high-impedance voltage sampling mode that
disables the digital control loop and allows sampling coherent to the vectors of the
digital pattern. The maximum sample frequency is 1 MHz. This AWG mode is
supported only for high-impedance voltage measurements. The coherent voltage
sampling mode is selected by function rdi.dc().connectSense().
Refer to paragraph "Timing relationship of AVI64 DC events" in AVI64 programming -
PMU operating mode for more information regarding the relationship of the force or
measure events in a pattern and the resulting DAC or ADC trigger of the channel front-
end.
PMU measure filter in coherent voltage sampling mode
The DGT features a low pass measure filter in both operating modes. The filter
frequency, which can be set by functions SPMU_PIN_TASK.measFilter() or
rdi.dc().measFilter(), is based on the sample frequency of 1 MHz that is the operating
frequency of the digital closed loop control. This means, that a compensated value has
to be programmed if another sample frequency is used in the coherent voltage
sampling mode:
DGT mode Low pass filter frequency to be programmed
Normal operating mode Target_filter_frequency
Coherent voltage sampling mode Target_filter_frequency * 1 MHz / Sample_frequency
where: Target_filter_frequency: The effective filter frequency to be set.
Sample_frequency: The sample frequency set by function rdi.dc().FS()
.
Note  Programming a compensated filter frequency as defined above is required
only for the coherent voltage sampling mode.

Measure filter settling time
The programmable digital low-pass measure filters for all ADCs behave like simple RC
filters. A short settling time is to be applied or some samples are to be ignored to settle
to an acceptable difference to the input signal.
Two operating modes are to be considered for estimating the required settling time or
number of samples:
Normal operating mode of the digital closed loop control
The continuous trigger for the ADCs is defined by the 1 MHz operating frequency
of the digital closed loop control. This mode is utilized for all measurement modes
except the coherent voltage sampling mode. The settling time of the measure filter
has to be considered in this mode.
Coherent voltage sampling mode
The trigger for the ADCs is defined only by DC measure events in a pattern. A
minimum number of samples as defined in the following formulas and examples
has to be considered in this mode.
The required settling time of the filter or the number of samples to be ignored depends
on the accepted maximum relative error and the effective filter frequency and is
calculated as follows:
Settling time = -1.0 * ln (Maximum relative error) / (2 * π * Filter frequency)
Number of samples = Settling time * Sample frequency
where: Maximum relative error = Maximum accepted relative error at the end of the settling time
Filter frequency = Effective filter frequency
Sample frequency = ADC sample frequency
ln = Natural logarithm

The functionality corresponds to the normal DGT mode of the PMU but the ADC trigger
is directly controlled by DC events in a pattern:
PMU DGT in normal sampling mode
The ADC trigger is controlled by the free running 1 MHz clock of the digital control

effective jitter of up to 1 us for the DGT samples.

The digital control loop is disabled in this mode. The trigger position for the ADC is
defined only by the DC events in the pattern. The time lag between the samples is
therefore always the same.

An AVI64 channel in the PMU operating mode features a high-speed AWG mode. The

Only voltage force mode without sensing is possible in the high-speed AWG mode. The
voltage drop on the wiring between the AVI64 output and the DUT is not compensated.
Therefore the generated voltages at the DUT pin may be lower than programmed.
In high-speed AWG mode the PMU use the force voltage ranges of the digital driver (8

Pattern frequency
The hardware limit for the sample clock of the high-speed AWG is 10 Msps.
The maximum pattern frequency is limited to 100 MHz in PMU or DPS operating mode.
As a consequence, with default pattern events, the maximal sample frequency is 3.125
MHz (100 MHz / 32 vectors).
In the AWG_X4 mode no sample frequency or sample period can be selected. That
implies that the count of samples is directly dependent on the pattern frequency. As
shown in the following calculation, this results in a maximum pattern frequency in
AWG_X4 mode of 80 MHz.
The max sample-clock frequency is 10 MHz, giving a period of 100 ns.
The AWG_X4 pattern event takes 32 pattern vectors and consists of 4 force values.
This means that one force value takes 8 pattern vectors, which then equates to the max
sample clock period of 100 ns.
1 pattern vector = 100 ns / 8 = 12.5 ns.
So the max pattern frequency for AWG_X4 events is 1 / 12.5 ns = 80 MHz.
Generally, the pattern frequency = 8 * sample-clock frequency.
CAUTION There is no error message or warning message in Smartest, if the
pattern frequency is higher than 80 MHz, so you must pay extra attention that the
pattern frequency is never higher than 80 MHz, as the waveform generation become
unreliable, which can lead to lost samples.

The maximum output current is the sum of the individual currents from each ganged
channel. The force lines (P#) and the sense lines (PS#, GS#) of all ganged channels have

AVI64 Use Case - SmartRDI - PMU sense only
connection
Each connected pin of an AVI64 channel adds a parasitic capacitive load to the related
DUT pin. The AVI64 PMUs provide a solution for minimizing this capacitive load by
routing the force output of the PMU via the sense pin PS# to sensitive high-speed DUT
pins. The force pin P# will not be connected with the sense only connection scheme.
Some limitations have to be considered for the single line low-capacitance connection
scheme:
The current capability is limited to 50 mA.
The voltage drop on the single PS# line is not compensated and therefore, the
voltage accuracy in current driving applications is limited.
The shared floating high-current unit cannot be connected.
The shared high-resolution arbitrary waveform generator cannot be connected.

AVI64 Use Case - SmartRDI - TMU basics
The AVI64 card features a time measurement unit (TMU) per pin that is available in the
PMU operating mode and in the Digital I/O operating mode.
The TMU is programmed in SmartRDI within a RDI_BEGIN() ... RDI_END() block. The
connection of the measure comparator is closed automatically before the SmartRDI
pattern is started and cannot be changed within the pattern. The measure mode can be
changed within the pattern.

TMU comparators
The AVI64 channels feature several different comparator inputs for the time
measurement.
There are two measure paths available with some additional options. The two measure
paths are the high-speed path, using the direct comparator signal and the high-
resolution path, using the ADC converted signal of the digital closed loop control with a
sampling frequency of 1 Mhz. If using the high-resolution comparator there is the
possibility to select a current comparator or a voltage comparator by setting the
threshold via functions rdi.tmu().vth(lowVoltageThreshold, highVoltageThreshold) or
rdi.tmu().ith(lowCurrentThreshold, highCurrentThreshold).

AVI64 Use Case - Best practice - Safe connect
and disconnect
Several facts have to be considered for safe connecting or disconnecting power
channels:
Each connection between a tester channel and pin of a DUT has at least parasitic
capacitance, parasitic inductivity and resistance.
The stimulation and the measurement of devices in the power / analog / control
sector is done in voltage regions of ±160 V and in current regions of ±10 A.
The test system cannot know what kind of wiring or additional device is on the DUT
board between the tester pin and the DUT pin.
The test system cannot know about the state of an active output pin of the DUT.
Careless proceeding of connect and disconnect can damage the DUT or the test
system.
Topic 151946
Topic 152529

Set up sequence: From DUT to tester channel
The following rules should be considered for connecting the DUT to a tester channel:
Know about the state of stimulation of all tester channels before you connect.
Know about the state of the DUT pin you need to connect to.
If relays or PMUX channels are used switch the relays which are nearest to DUT first,
the relays nearest to tester switch last!
Connect always with a voltage difference of zero between the tester channel and
the DUT pin!
The usage of the rdi.dc().preCharge() feature of AVI64 and PVI8 is highly
recommended.
AVI64 provides in addition to the value based pre-charging the Smart Connect
feature that is also controlled by the rdi.dc().preCharge() API and selected by
parameter TA::SAFE_CON: The voltage at the DUT is sensed and the PMU is
automatically set to the measured voltage before the pin is connected.
Example for AVI64 and PVI8: rdi.dc().pin(...).preCharge(0.0 V)...;
Example only for AVI64:
rdi.dc().pin(...).preCharge(TA::SAFE_CON)...;
Wait an appropriate time until all settings had time to reach the DUT pin.
Take the measurements according to the specifications' needs.
Set down sequence: From instrument to DUT
The following rules should be considered for disconnecting a tester channel from
the DUT:
Always consider "What is happening next?".
Disconnect always with a voltage difference of zero between the tester channel and
DUT pin!
Force 0.0 V and take a wait for discharging components and circuit before
disconnecting or
force to a defined voltage level where an active output pin of the DUT reaches a
relaxed state.
If relays or PMUX channels are used switch the relays which are nearest to tester
first, the relays nearest to DUT switch last.

In case the measurement range (Clamp-range) should be switched over several steps,
you must watch that there is not too much time between clamp and range
programming. Otherwise, the ranges must be switched step-by-step. The reason is that
the minimum allowed clamp value to be programmed is a certain percentage of the
range, which is needed to keep the control loop in a stable condition. If the

it is possible to bypass this.

profiler functionality from Hardware view (continuous sampling) it seems there are
spikes, when range is changed. A range change takes less than 50 µs for AVI64.

The "conditional go to" provides the functions for specifying and executing conditional
jumps into different labels of a pattern‑based on pass / fail evaluations.
In general the CoGo test is pathing through a predefined pattern, depending on the
PASS / FAIL state by use of match loops.
There are various CoGo methods supported by the RDI programming. The user can
define the program flow by himself or use predefined linear or binary CoGo searches,
which can be used for measuring threshold voltages.
Three approaches are available to implement a "conditional go to" within a CoGo node
of an RDI_BEGIN() / RDI_END() block:
Comparator
The comparator of the related channel is set up for the PASS / FAIL decision. The
example code
defines that tat the high-speed voltage comparator of "myAnalogPin" has to be
used for the PASS / FAIL decision. The comparator is set up as window comparator
with a pass range from lowVal to highVal. This approach is to be used for AVI64
pins in PMU operating mode.
The "conditional go to" on an AVI64 channel supports all comparator types that are
available for the time measurement unit (TMU).
Digital pin compare
A short pattern is inserted within a CoGo node to perform the PASS / FAIL decision.
The example code
uses a pattern of 10 vectors of "X" with only vector 5 set to "L". This approach is to
be used for AVI64 pins in Digital I/O operating mode.
Existing pattern
An existing pattern can be called within the CoGo node. The pattern is to be
implemented as follows:
This approach can be used for AVI64 pins in PMU operating mode or in Digital I/O
operating mode.
rdi.dc().pin("myAnalogPin").vMeas().limit(lowVal, highVal).compMod
rdi.smartVec().pin("myDigitalPin").defaultVec("X").vecLength(10).w
rdi.func().label("myCheckPattern").execute();

Vector pipeline
Because there is a big vector pipeline before the PASS / FAIL decision in a pattern, it is
important to wait after match loop condition for the PASS / FAIL decision. The best is to
use rdi.cogo().wait(xxx); which gives a warning, if the wait time is lower than the
Pass/Fail pipeline.
Multi-port CoGo
If any other measurement than the CoGo is done, the CoGo test will always FAIL.
Therefore the CoGo port has to be defined in a separate sequence.
Waveform Definition for CoGo Path-Pin
To retrieve results value from a CoGo block a pattern path pin can be defined and
utilized. The pattern path pin has to be set up in the level file and has to be connected
using the related member functions of class rdi.hwRelay().
Capture waveforms must be defined for the pattern path pin. The required waveform
definition is different for the linear CoGo search test and the binary CoGo search test:
Linear CoGo search test
Binary CoGo search test
For more information refer to rdi.cogo().pathPin().

An AVI64 channel can be configured for applications that require a seamless integration

Digital I/O pin characteristics
The AVI64 pin does not have a load bridge. If the pin is used as output, the driver can be
used to generate a 3rd voltage level vt (pull-up or pull-down via 50 Ohm).
If the pin is defined as IO pin in the pin configuration, the drive edge in the wavetable
has to be programmed to Z during compare. Otherwise the DUT output will be loaded
by the driver (last used level) via the 50 Ohm.
Switching to HIZ (open driver relay) takes 10us and is programmed via driving edge in
the wavetable.

The AVI64 has the possibility to use the HiResolution Comparator (voltage or current) for
digital measurements with the time measurement unit (TMU).
The analog bandwidth of the high resolution comparator is limited to 250 kHz (versus
high speed comparator bandwidth 50 MHz). In contrast to the high speed comparator
the high resolution comparator can reduce the measure bandwidth by programming the
measurement filter. In digital mode there is no API for the measure filter, therefore the
last programmed value from a DC-setup is valid. If not programmed the default is 250
kHz.

This enhanced accuracy can only be reached by executing the DC update calibration.
This calibration is valid for a time span of one week.
Because of the requirement of a regularly repetition of the DC update calibration, it
might be useful to do this automatically. This automatic calibration can be done by the
Test Cell Control Tool (TCCT).
For executing the DC update calibration automatically by the TCCT the following items
are required:
1. Script hp83_startCal (the script for executing several calibrations manually,
included by SmarTest installation)
2. A script which calls hp83_startCal
3. TCCT
4. Recipe file
The script hp83_startCal is a script which is installed on each workstation which has
SmarTest installed. The automatic DC update calibration by the TCCT has to be done by
executing a script which calls the script hp83_startCal.
The TCCT is designed for production engineering and it cooperates with SmarTest to
execute the testflow. An important part of the TCCT for the automatic DC update
calibration is the recipe file.
The recipe file includes several elements. The element states defines the insertion point
to execute some scripts. Within this element the DC update calibration script can be
executed with a defined action, in the following example before the action LOT_CREATE.
Examples

AVI64 Use Case - GND-Sense modulation
Sometimes it is needed to generate precise AC signal with a small Vpp on top of a
supply voltage with relative high DC value. For this purpose the channel specific ground
sense input of AVI64 channels can be modulated by a high-resolution voltage AWG. It is
possible to shift the AVI64 ground sense input up ±5 V from the common DUT board
GND.
To increase the signal resolution a voltage divider on the GND sense path can be
implemented to use the high-resolution voltage AWG in full scale range (FSR). This
voltage divider can be used additionally as a low pass filter (LPF) for the modulation
signal by adding a capacitor.
Advantage of modulating the GND sense input:
For AC-signal up to ±4 V the shared high-resolution voltage AWG of the AVI64
channel group can be used.
The resolution of the AC part of the signal depends not on the full scale signal
range of the DC part.
Any DC offset within the AVI64 voltage range is possible.
Disadvantage of modulating the GND sense input:
A second channel is required to generate the modulation signal.

If the programmed load capacitance is lower than the actually used capacitive load or
not programmed (default = 0 nF), the signal regulation will be slower than expected, but
it will not oscillate. Additional you may detect that in voltage force mode the measured
current when changing the voltage (load/unload the capacitance) is lower than the

from programmed capacitance.
If you use the rdi.dc().loadCap() function and change the effective capacitive load (for
example, switch by relay) when an AVI64 channel is connected, pay attention to
following rules:
Reducing the capacitance:
1. Set the programmed load capacitance to the lower value
2. Switch the capacitor to the lower value
Increasing the capacitance:
1. Switch the capacitor to the higher value
2. Set the programmed load capacitance to the higher value
The effective capacitor value can be influenced by the parasitic series resistance of
the switch. Therefore use low resistive switches or consider the effective capacitor in
the programmed load capacitance: The effective capacitor value may be lower than
expected. Otherwise you may generate oscillations!
When changing the voltage on a capacitive load, changing to a higher current
range until signal is settled may result in shorter test time than changing the load
capacitance and keeping the original current range.

AVI64 Use Case - Kelvin test unit
The AVI64 card features a Kelvin test unit (or sense-connection test unit), which can be
used to verify that the force lines and sense lines are connected together on the DUT
board or at the DUT pins. The Kelvin test unit is available per channel for the P# to PS#
connection and the GND to GS# connection.
The Kelvin test unit utilizes a GND referenced current source between the sense and
force wiring of the AVI64 channel. Therefore, two measurements are automatically
performed to ensure that open connections can be detected even if a DUT pin has an
internal low impedance connection to ground.
Basic data of the AVI64 Kelvin test unit:
The Kelvin test unit is available per channel.
The threshold for the pass/fail decision is about 5 kΩ.
The test current is about 100 µA.
The maximum capacitance between the force lines and the corresponding sense
lines is 5 nF.
The set up and set down of the test is performed in parallel on all selected pins.
Three measurements are serially performed for the P# pin, the PS# pin and the GS#
pin.
Testing eight AVI64 pins requires a test time of about 10 ms per site.
The test can be performed only in the disconnected state of the selected pins.

AVI64 Use Case - Measurement filter
coherent / non coherent
The measurement filter of the AVI64 channels is a digital filter. Depending on the
previously measured signal, the effect on the measured signal is like putting a low-pass
filter (LPF) into the signal-path.
The filter shows different behavior for the normal sampling mode and the coherent
sampling mode:
Normal sampling mode
The ADC trigger is controlled by the free running 1 MHz clock of the digital control
loop. The continuous stream of measured values that is the input for the digital
control loop is also used as data source for the DGT samples. This results in an
effective jitter of up to 1 us for the DGT samples.
The LPF filter is continuously working and get its data from the continuous stream
of ADC values.
Coherent voltage sampling mode
The digital control loop is disabled in this mode. The trigger position for the ADC is
defined only by the DC events in the pattern. The time lag between the samples is
therefore always the same. The coherent sampling mode is selected by
rdi.dc().connectState(TA::HIZ_COHERENT).
The LPF filter gets input data synchronous to the DC events in the pattern.
The difference between coherent sampling and non-
coherent sampling is that the filter is effective working
always in normal measure mode and in coherent measure
mode only if it is sampling.
 
Therefore for steady state signal, you have to wait until the signal is present in normal
mode and in coherent mode you have to ignore the first periods of the signal.
Topic 151950

The diagram above shows a measured signal (coherent sampling, filter = 3 kHz, signal
frequency = 3 kHz), wait time before sampling 6 periods of the generated signal.
In coherent sampling mode the filter transient effect is always present when starting the
sampling because the digital filter gets data only when sampling has been started.
In non-coherent mode you will get steady state of filter with wait time on a present
signal, too (1MHz internal clock is independent when sampling non coherent).

Calculating the filter setting for coherent sampling
The time constant for filter swing in (wait time until filter is settled) depends on the
sampling mode and the actual sampling frequency.
How many samples should be ignored?
depends on filter frequency and sample rate
the effective filter frequency depends on sample rate, too
The number of ignored samples depends only on the programmed filter
frequency!
Swing in to one time constant (Tau = R * C) = 1 MHz / (programmed_filter_frequency)
Example:
FS = 976kHz, effectiveFilter = 20kHz => programmedFilter = 20.48kHz
Settling to 14 Tau: 14 * 1 MHz / 20.48kHz = 684 samples ==> after 684 samples the
filter is settled with 14 Tau.

Defining context specific timing and levels

Context per test suite
The context of a test suite is defined with its primary settings of Timing and Level.
Usually the pattern is based on the same context.
When using SmartRDI the patterns will be generated within the first run but if there is
no pattern defined, the context for the pattern is detected as DEFAULT.

PMU operating mode and DEFAULT context
Note  An AVI64 channel that should be configured for the PMU operating mode
and for the Digital I/O operating mode requires that the PMU operating mode is
configured in the DEFAULT mode context. Default mode context means the context
that is named DEFAULT.
As soon as you are using a channel of AVI64 in Digital I/O operating mode and in DC
mode, you must define two mode contexts. For example, if one test suite is using a
channel in DC mode and another test suite is using the same channel in Digital I/O
operating mode, then different mode contexts must be used. If a channel of the AVI64 is
used in different mode contexts, the DEFAULT context must be "dc" and "SIG".
Otherwise, the switching of context will not work.
CAUTION If the mode context is used to switch between the PMU operating
mode and the Digital I/O operating mode, every test suite in the test program must
include a pattern with the appropriate context. The pattern can be empty and does
not need to be called.

AVI64 Use Case - RDSon test
When a power MOSFET is in the on-state it exhibits a resistive behavior between the
drain and source terminals. This resistance is called RDSon for "drain to source
resistance in on-state".
What is the RDSon test?
Typically pattern controlled sequence:
1. Execute digital pattern to switch the FET to the on-state (FET-on)
2. Force high current by power source (iForce)
3. Measure the voltage drop by power source's differential voltmeter
4. Force off power source (iForce)
5. Execute digital pattern to switch off the FET (FET-off)
6. Retrieve the results (vMeas)
7. Calculate the (R)esistance of the (D)rain to (S)ource path when the
FET is (on):
RDSon = vMeas / iForce

AVI64 Use Case - Semi-parallel usage of
shared resources
AVI64 resources like the floating differential voltmeter, the floating high-current unit and
the high-resolution arbitrary waveform generator are shared between for pin groups of
eight channels.
In case these resources are shared between different sites a parallel execution is not
possible! Instead of pure serial test program execution, the program can be executed
semi parallel to allow high throughput without conflict due to shared resources. The
user has to define group of sites, which can be executed in parallel.

AVI64 Use Case - Tester memory usage -
how to deal with insufficient tester memory
The AVI64 has enough memory for most applications, but in some special cases, for
example when sampling many waveforms, the memory may not be sufficient. These
special cases will be described in this use case.
If you receive the error message
ERROR: FTST? - CExternalException (Insufficient channel memory for
DPS/DC measurement results.)
while executing the testflow, it is recommended that you open the Tester Memory
Usage view. With this tool it is easy to identify the affected channel.
The following example is forcing and capturing a very large waveform on the "AVI_01"
pin. After executing the measurement, only a few bytes of memory remain. When
another test suite is executed (which does not need to capture large waveforms) the
error message mentioned above appears. The reason for this error can be extracted
quickly from the Tester Memory Usage view.
The "AVI_01" pin does not have any memory left. This error message will not only
appear when there is no more memory left. It can also be displayed when there are only
a few bytes left. The same error message can also appear if all pins have enough
memory but no digital_default_result_area_size is defined in the .technology file.
This error can be avoided by using the RESULT_AREA_CONFIG_SET() test method API.
This API provides access to some functions, which allows the user to handle result area
configurations.

Functionality
Each of the 128 or 64 channels of a DC Scale DPS128/DPS64 cards can:
source and sink current at a programmed voltage,
measure the voltages and currents supplied,
supply power to external circuits on a DUT board,
be programmed in a test suite for a certain test,
be shared between different sites (channel sharing),
be ganged to increase the supply current,
do connectivity checks,
check the status of the device power supply.

Automatic down-ranging
DPS128/DPS64 channels feature automatic down-ranging for current measurements.
Automatic down-ranging means that the current range is automatically changed to the
best fit range for the measurement and restored to the original range after the
measurement.
Two parameters define whether the automatic down-ranging is performed or not:
1. The force / clamp current range:
Can be set explicitly or (if not defined)
is automatically derived from the forced or clamped value.
2. The current measurement range:
Can be set explicitly or (if not defined)
is automatically derived from the pass/fail thresholds.
Automatic down-ranging is performed only if the current measurement range is lower
than the force / clamp current range regardless whether the ranges have been set
explicitly or have been selected automatically.
Automatic down-ranging is supported for both code‑based programming using the
SPMU_TASK and DPS_TASK test method APIs and the pattern‑based programming using
the DC events and is also supported by SmartRDI.
Capacitor requirements
External capacitors on the DUT board improve the DPS stability and loadstep response
and reduce oscillations and noise. For more information, refer to DPS128 / DPS64
capacitor requirements in the electrical design rules for the DPS128/DPS64 section.
Channel sharing
You can share the same DC Scale channel between several sites.
This allows you to save DPS channels and to supply external circuits on the DUT board.
See also Test Method Programs and Sharing Channels Between Several Sites.
Clamping and forcing current
In the current force mode, the DPS128 applies a positive or negative voltage depending
on the sign of the programmed force current and uses the clamp current functionality to
limit the actual current to the target current. The minimum clamp current mentioned
below therefore also applies to the forced minimum current.

Comparators
Each HC channel of the DC Scale DPS128/DPS64 card features a pair of two high-
bandwidth comparators connected to the sense lines. They work similarly to digital
comparators and can therefore be used similarly as a digital output channel (for
example for match loops).
Note  This feature is not supported on DPS128-HV channels.
The comparators are supported both in DPS operating mode and in PMU operating
mode.
They can be connected to the voltage sensor (Vsense) or the current sensor (Isense),
which monitor the voltage on the sense line or the output current of the channel. See
also the DPS128 / DPS64 hardware overview.
In voltage compare mode the DC accuracy is around ±10 mV (typical) with a minimum
detectable pulse width of 1  μs.
In current compare mode the DC accuracy is ±10 % (typical) of the selected current
range with a minimum detectable pulse width in dependency to the range. It is 1 μs for
the highest range (1 A) and scaling by factor 10 for each 2nd range going from the
highest to lower ranges (i.e. 200 mA, 25 mA, 2.5 mA, ...).
Comparators are addressed via special operation modes controlled by the
DPS_AUX_TASK test method API.
Note that on AVI64, DPS128/64, and FVI16 you cannot execute a current compare on a
ganged group of channels if the group is in unganged mode. Already activated
comparators are silently disabled in unganged mode. A user notification (Error or
warning) is omitted in this case, to avoid any interrupt in the testflow. The previous state
of the comparators is automatically restored after the ganged group has been restored.
Current force and measure ranges
The DPS128/DPS64 current force and measure ranges are linked. The required down-
ranging before a measurement and up-ranging after the measurement has an impact on
test times, both in DPS mode and in PMU mode. See also DPS128 / DPS64 specific setup
tasks.

Ganging channels
To achieve a higher output current, you can operate multiple channels of DC Scale
DPS128/DPS64 cards in parallel, known as ganging. Ganging is the combining of
multiple DPS channels to provide a higher current than a single DPS channel could
provide.
The actual ganging, that is the physical parallel connection, is done on the DUT board.
For details see Connecting DPS channels in parallel.
To set up a DPS128/DPS64 channel gang you use the Pin configuration tool.
You can gang any number of successive channels of the same type within a
DPS128/DPS64 card. Ganged channels must be located on the same card. You
cannot gang across DPS128/DPS64 cards.
You can configure these successive channels in up to 64 gang groups in a DPS128,
and 32 gang groups in a DPS64.
For details on the setup procedure see Defining DC Scale Pins.
For the firmware commands see DFPS, DFPS? - (DeFine Power Supply) for ganging in
DPS operating mode and DFPN, DFPN? - (DeFine Pin Name) for ganging in PMU
operating mode.
Each gang group consists of a master channel and one or more slave channels. The
master channel distributes two analog signals to the slave channels. One signal is the
target voltage on the output, and the second is a voltage that represents the current of
the master. The slave channels will adjust their own voltage to match the current of the
master channel.
Ganging supplies higher currents to a device. To avoid a negative effect on measure-
current accuracy, for example for IDD-measurements, you can temporarily ungang
channels during measurement. The unganging process differs for the DPS and PMU
operating modes. For details see Measuring current or voltage in DPS operating mode
and Measuring current or voltage in PMU operating mode.
For measurements in DPS mode, channels must be sequentially unganged starting from
the last channel and reconnected after measurement.
Licensing
The device power supply cards DC Scale DPS128 and DC Scale DPS64 require no license.

Measurement modes
DC Scale DPS128/DPS64 cards support voltage and current measurements in both the
DPS and PMU operating modes.
For measurements in DPS operating mode see Measuring current or voltage in DPS
operating mode.
For measurements in DPS mode, ganged channels must be sequentially unganged
starting from the last channel and reconnected after measurement.
For measurements in PMU operating mode see Measuring current or voltage in PMU
operating mode. These are:
current measurements
unganged current measurements
voltage measurement
high-impedance voltage measure mode
The PMU operating mode is used to test PMIC (power management integrated circuit)
regulator outputs, mostly sequentially, and requires connect/disconnect per
measurement. The impact of relay settling times is significant.
Minimum clamp current distance
DPS128 requires a minimum clamp current to work properly. Therefore, the clamp
current cannot be set to 0.0 A. The minimum programmable clamp current is
20 % of the selected current range for the HC variant, and
10 % of the selected current range for the HV variant.
For details, refer to
Supply voltage / current range specifications (high current) and
Supply voltage / current range specifications (high voltage).
The specification tables linked above define the range as "minimum to maximum". The
minimum value on the left is the minimum programmable clamp current value.
If necessary, SmarTest automatically adjusts the clamp current settings to the minimum
value as defined in the current specifications and displays the following warning in the

Clamp current limit is smaller than minimum value and will be auto-cor

Operating modes
DC Scale DPS128/DPS64 cards have two operating modes:
DPS operating mode (DPS+)
In DPS operating mode you can use DC Scale DPS128/DPS64 cards like a standard
DPS, to supply devices with power during the execution of a testflow.
To find a summary of all supported resource parameters in the level file, refer to
DPSPINS resources.
PMU operating mode (SIG)
In PMU operating mode you can use DC Scale DPS128/DPS64 cards like a standard
PMU to temporarily supply power for a single test suite or for a group of test suites.
A DPS128/DPS64 channel can be configured either for the DPS operating mode or for
the PMU operating mode but not for both.
In both operating modes each of the 128 or 64 channels of every power supply card can
source and sink current at a programmed voltage,
measure the voltages and currents supplied,
supply power to external circuits on a DUT board,
be programmed in a test suite for a certain test,
be shared between different sites (channel sharing),
be ganged to increase the supply current,
do connectivity checks,
check the status of the device power supply.
The DPS operating mode is a superset of the PMU operating mode and has some
additional capabilities. Only in DPS operating mode the DC Scale power supply cards
can
take part in connect and disconnect sequences, and
take part in the set activation.
Note  In PMU operating mode a DC Scale DPS128/DPS64 card does not take part in
standard connect and disconnect sequences, and cannot take part in the set
activation, although you can add DC Scale DPS128/DPS64 cards to user-defined
connect and disconnect sequences.
For further details see DPS128 / DPS64 in DPS operating mode and DPS128 / DPS64 in

Profiling in Hardware view
Profiling (DC profiling) allows you to measure and display current and voltage
waveforms during pattern execution in the Hardware perspective. Current and voltage
profiling is supported for all channels, both in DPS mode and in PMU mode.
On DC Scale AVI64, DPS128/64, FVI16, PVI8 and UHC4T cards, profiling for multiport
setups does not stop when the DPS part is finished. On these cards, profiling stops when
the longest running port is finished. This gives the capability to profile the supply
voltages/currents during the complete execution. In case you want to reduce memory
consumption, you could put DPS pins into an empty port.
For the DC Scale DPS128/DPS64 cards, changing the current measurement range for
profiling is not supported. That is, the measureRange parameter of the
DC_PROFILING_DEFINE and DC_PROFILING_ON APIs is ignored when the measureType
parameter is set to TM::CURRENT. The profiling measurements are performed in the
selected clamp current range.
Note  DC profiling of the current is not supported if a pin is in UNGANG mode.
The profiling sample rate is up to 100 ksps for up to 16 channels. To achieve this rate,
the channels must be distributed over 16 pin groups, where each pin group consists of 8
pins (1-8, 9-16, 17-24, ..., 113-128).
In case of more than one channel per pin group, the profiling sample rate is 50 ksps. See
also DPS128/DPS64 specifications.
Note that the DPS128/DPS64, when starting the sequencer with the SQST RUN firmware
command or with the SEQUENCER_STATUS run() test method, cannot execute dynamic
and static DC actions in parallel. Use profiling for measurements in parallel to a dynamic
pattern.

Sense connection test
The DPS128 channels feature a sense connection test unit, which is also know as Kelvin
test unit.
Kelvin test or sense connection test means that the connection from the force lines to
the sense lines on the DUT board or at the DUT pins is verified with a small test current
applied. A PASS/FAIL result is returned.
The Kelvin test unit is available in the PMU operating mode and in the DPS operating
mode.
The Kelvin test unit applies a small test current to the tested force to sense (FS)
connection and measures the voltage drop between the two lines. The measured
voltage is used as criterion for the pass/fail decision and should be near 0.0 V for a good
FS connection. The Kelvin test unit of a DPS128 supports the test of the P# to PS#
connection and the test of the common GND to GS# connection.
Basic data of the DPS128 Kelvin test / sense connection test unit:
PS# pin GS# pin
Threshold for the pass/fail decision: 3.4 kΩ (typ.) 20 kΩ (typ.)
Test current: 44 μA (typ.) 50 μA (typ.)
Note  The purpose of the Kelvin test unit is to ensure that when the DUT is
contacted, the high-impedance sense line is connected to the force line at the DUT
with a sufficiently low contact resistance. Due to the high input impedance of the
sense lines, the fixed threshold of some kilo-Ohms will be sufficiently low.
The Kelvin test unit is the only resource that can perform a reliable sense connection
test with a defined test current applied.
Since connections and hardware on the DUT board can sabotage the test of the
sense connections, we recommend that you check the functionality of the test
without DUT and with open sense connections. All tested sense connections must
fail in this verification.
The purpose of the Kelvin test unit is not to check the low impedance force
connections. For the DPS128-HC variant, force connections can be checked by the
Voltage drop measurement in combination with a high test current forced by the
PMU.

This force connection test requires that the contact resistance of the sense
lines already has been verified.
Attention: An inadequate sense line connection does not necessarily mean that a
voltage drop test fails. The input bias current of the line may falsify the measurement
and mask another fatal error like a high voltage drop on the force line.

CAUTION The DPS128 forces the test current via one of the tested lines, the FS
connection, and via the other tested line to ground. One of the lines may be
internally connected to ground for the test. Therefore, the DUT must be powered
down before the Kelvin test (or sense connection test) is started in disconnected
mode.
For information on how to program a sense connection test, refer to functions
checkKelvinStatusParallel() and HW_STATE.checkKelvinStatus() of class HW_STATE.

Surge tracker
The surge tracker monitors the voltage via sense lines or the output current. It is
implemented on the comparator pair of the DPS128/DPS64.
Note  This feature is not supported on DPS128-HV channels.
Once the surge tracker is turned on, it monitors unless being turned off. Connect or
disconnect sequences do not reset it. In a typical use scenario you activate the surge
tracker in the very beginning of a testflow and check the status at the end of it.
Voltage or current surges are detected against min. and max. values. The surge tracker
always checks against both high (positive) and low (negative) thresholds, which can be
set individually. Two flags indicate if the high and low thresholds have been exceeded.
These flags are latched (stored) and can be retrieved any time in the testflow.

Test processor, memory, and data analysis features
Setup and measurement sequences are controlled by test processors. A test
processor features eight cores, each controlling one channel.
The test processor memory is shared between setups, testpoints, waveforms, digital
patterns, and sample data or measurement results.
The memory available per channel for the test program is approximately 24 MB for
a typical setup.
Several alarm flags are available to indicate irregular operating conditions.
Hardware based averaging is available for better accuracy and throughput.
A built-in result analysis is available that checks the measurement data against user
specified test limits.

Voltage drop measurement
The HC variant of the DPS128 features a voltage drop measurement unit, which is also
known as Kelvin measurement unit.
Voltage drop measurement means that the voltage drop on the force lines can be
measured while a significant current is flowing.
The voltage drop measurement unit of the HC variant allows you measuring the voltage
drop on the P# line and on the GND line. Measuring the voltage drop ensures that the
force connections to the DUT have a sufficiently low resistance for the required current.
It also ensures that there is enough voltage headroom left for proper work of the power
stage.
The drawing below shows an example of an optional voltage drop measurement
performed on the supply line of the DUT while the DUT is powered. The current for the
test is defined by the DUT. For this test, you must first apply the supply voltage to the
DUT in VFIM mode of DPS128. After the current has been stabilized, you can measure
the current, change to the VFVM mode and measure the voltage drop. For this test, the
DUT‑defined current must be high enough for a reliable result and must be stable for
the time of the current and voltage drop measurements.
DPS128 Kelvin measurement operating principle
If the DPS128 is not used to supply the DUT but, for example, to test a low‑side switch
of the DUT or another load with a higher current, we recommend measuring the voltage
drop with a smaller test current before performing the high‑current test. The voltage
drop measurement can then be set up in the IFVM mode of DPS128.
The voltage drop on the force lines (P#) and ground (GND) is rated from the pogo pin
to the F-S connection on the DUT board or at the DUT pins. The internal voltage drop
needs not to be considered.
Note  The resistance of the force lines is defined by contact resistance of the pogo
pins, the traces on the DUT board, and by the DUT socket or probes. Contaminated
pogo pads and DUT sockets or insufficient contact pressure of the probes may
significantly increase the voltage drop. For ganged channels, the voltage drop is
measured on the master channel.

For ganged channels, the voltage drop is
measured on the master channel.
Note  A sufficiently low contact resistance of the sense connections is a
precondition for a reliable voltage drop measurement. We therefore strongly
recommend performing a sense connection tests once per test run using the Sense
connection test.
For information on how to use the voltage drop measurement unit, refer to function
SPMU_PIN_TASK.connectState() of class SPMU_TASK and to function
measurementMode() of class DPS_PIN_TASK. In SmartRDI, the voltage drop

measurement is set up by functions rdi.dc().vMeasForceDrop() and
rdi.dc().vMeasReturnDrop().
Voltage drop measurements are also supported by the measurement dialog of the
Hardware view for DPS and VI pins. Voltage drop measurements are labeled
"Kelvin_High" and "Kelvin_Low" in the DPS128‑specific version of the dialog.

DPS128 / DPS64 power budget
The DPS128/DPS64 card features two power domains with a dedicated power budget.
Each domain is able to deliver half of the overall power budget. SmarTest limits the
overall power usage, so that the power budget of each domain is not exceeded. Any
violation will trigger an error message.
Power budget
For a DPS128/DPS64 card, the maximum total power budget of the raw voltage supplies
is 426 W. This budget is distributed equally to two power domains. Within the two
power domains, the available budget of 213 W is shared by the output stages of 64
channels (DPS128) or 32 channels (DPS64).
Note  The available power budget mentioned above, is available at the output
stages of the power domains.
The total power to be assessed for the individual channels therefore includes not
only the power at the DUT, but also the internal power dissipation of the output
stage, the power loss at the internal resistor for current measurements and the
power loss of internal traces and the pogo cable.
We therefore recommend using the DPS128 Power Calculator for calculating the
total power consumption and the utilization of the power budgets.
For high current channels, the voltage range needs to be adapted accordingly to
minimize the consumed power. For more information refer to section Limiting
voltage ranges below.
For more information, refer to section "3 Power Budget" of the DC Scale DPS128/64
HC/HV Cookbook

DPS128 V-I curves and board power
restrictions
The V-I curves of the two types of DPS128 channels are quite different. Despite the fact
of different voltage ranges and less current capability for HV type of channels, the HV
type of channels do not have any current limit to voltage dependency over their voltage
operating range as there is for HC type. In other words a HV type of channel can provide
its maximum current limit for all possible voltages over the whole operating range.
Topic 147810

Output characteristics
For HC channels, the maximum current limit depends on the voltage range. For a
specified voltage range of 2.5 V the maximum current limit is 1 A, while for a specified
voltage range of 7 V the maximum current is 500 mA. For voltage ranges between 7 V
and 2.5 V, the maximum current limit decreases in a linear manner, for example, for a
specified voltage range of 4 V the maximum current is 0.833 A.
To achieve 3 A @ 4V it is required to gang:

4 channels, if voltage range is set to 4 V
6 channels, if voltage range is set to 7 V (default)
Refer to DPS128 voltage ranges for more details.
What also needs to be taken into consideration is that the V-I curve cannot be mapped
one-to-one to a complete DPS128 board - the maximum current limit of a channel
cannot be applied to all channels of a board in parallel. This restriction is driven by the
overall available power budget of a board.
