FVI16 programming - Power budget
management
The power budget management allows you assigning power budget or energy budget
to individual channels according to the needs of the testflow. If the power budget
management is activated, only channels that exceed the assigned budget will be
disconnected.
The power budget management is supported only for FVI16 channels in PMU operating
mode.
Disabling and enabling the FVI16 power budget management
The power budget management functionality is enabled by default.
For special cases, the power budget management functionality may be disabled and
enabled by Test method API SET_POWERBUDGET_CONTROL().
CAUTION Disabling the power budget management significantly increases the
risk of errors or other incorrect behavior of the test program: The maximum total
power and the total consumable energy budget are still monitored but a single
channel at a faulty DUT will have an effect on other channels or (passing) sites if the
power budget management is disabled.We strongly recommend, always keeping the
power budget management functionality enabled.
CAUTION The power budget management is always enabled for all FVI16 cards
or disabled for all FVI16 cards. Enabling or disabling the power budget management
for selected cards or channels is not supported.

Transfer of budget within the channel group
In PMU operating mode, the transfer of assigned power budget or energy budget is
supported within the channel groups. The assigned budget of the old channel must first
be lowered before the budget of the receiving channel can be increased.
Note  You can transfer power budget or energy budget only within the two channel

group is not supported.

Offline power and energy analyzer
We provide an analyzer that helps you offline calculating the utilization of the power
and energy budget. The HTML page supports defining and calculating all relevant
parameters for handling the two budgets. For more information and the download link,
refer to section Offline power and energy analyzer - FVI16 PowerAnalyst in FVI16 power
budget and energy budget.

Power budget monitoring and status flags
The assigned power budget and energy budget can be changed by static programming
using, for example, the SPMU_TASK member functions or within a pattern run using the
EVENT_PBUDGET. The same structure applies to functions that define the consumed
power and energy like EVENT_COMPLIANCE or EVENT_CF.
Therefore, monitoring of the assigned and consumed power budget and energy budget
can only be done by the channel controllers of the hardware. There is no monitoring or
feedback supported in offline mode.
The following status flags relate to the power budget and energy budget:
Battery full
The flag indicates the charge condition of the on-board energy storages. The flag is
for information only.
For more information and the related APIs, refer to Battery full in FVI16 status flags.
Power budget 1
The on-board energy storage of the related channel group is almost empty. The
threshold for this flag is 10 % of the full capacity. The flag is for information only. The
flag is available per channel if the power budget management is activated.
For more information and the related APIs, refer to Power budget 1 in FVI16 status
flags.
Power budget 2
A setup error has been detected: The assigned power budget or the assigned energy
budget exceed the available budget. The flag is for information only.
For more information and the related APIs, refer to Power budget 2 in FVI16 status
flags.
Power budget 3
The virtual energy storage of the related channel is almost empty. The threshold for
this flag is 10 % of the assigned energy budget. The flag is for information only.
For more information and the related APIs, refer to Power budget 3 in FVI16 status
flags.
Low headroom
The required power budget or energy budget exceeds the available budget. The
related channel is disconnected if the power budget management functionality is
activated. Otherwise, all channels of the related group will be disconnected.
For more information and the related APIs, refer to Low headroom in FVI16 status
flags.

CAUTION Monitoring of the assigned and consumed power budget and energy
budget can be done only by the channel controllers of the hardware and is therefore
supported only in online mode. There is no monitoring or feedback supported in
offline mode.
We strongly recommend, checking the status flags that are for information only and
do not result in disconnected channels. The check should be done at least once at
the end of a testflow. The following flags should be checked:
Power budget 1
Power budget 2
Power budget 3
We also recommend, checking the charging state of the on-board energy storages
before high-current tests are started. The related flag is Battery full.

Charging the on-board energy storages
With activated power budget management, the assigned energy budget of a channel
corresponds to a virtual energy storage within the on-board energy storage of the eight
channel group. This virtual energy storage must be recharged after the assigned energy
has been consumed.
All the assigned power budget that is not used by a channel will be used to recharge the
on-board energy storage of the related eight channel group unless it is fully charged.
The channel can again consume the assigned energy budget as soon as the on-board
storage has been charged with the assigned energy budget of the budget.
Increasing the assigned energy budget of a channels by APIs
rdi.dc().pulseEnergyBudget(), SPMU_PIN_TASK.pulseEnergy() or
EVENT_PBUDGET.pulseEnergy() requires some time for charging the virtual energy
storage of the channel. The required time corresponds to the energy to be charged and
the available power budget of the channel.
The time for charging the virtual energy storage depends on the assigned energy
budget and the available power budget:
Big energy budget and small power budget: Long time.
Small energy budget and big power budget: Short time.
The time for charging a virtual energy storage can be calculated as follows:
time = energy / power
with energy = Energy in Joule or Watt-second to charge
power = Assigned and available power in Watt
time = The time in seconds to increase or decrease the charging level of the virtual energy storage to
the new energy level
The formula above applies only for the virtual energy storages with enabled power
budget management. For recharging the physical energy storage of an eight‑channel
group, the tolerance in capacitance must be considered. Recharging the 1.6 J of a fully
discharged physical energy storage needs maximum 15 ms if the complete power
budget of 200 W is available.

Application notes
Channels in high-voltage mode or high-impedance voltage measure mode
Channels in high-voltage mode or in high-impedance voltage measure mode are
also to be considered for the power budget management:
Power budget: The utilized power budget is not monitored in these modes but a
minimum power budget of 4.0 W must be assigned.
Energy budget: Channels in these modes cannot utilize the energy budget. The
assigned energy budget can be set to 0.0 J.
Increase both the energy budget and the power budget for high-power pulses
Increasing only the assigned energy budget of a channel will increase the time for
charging the virtual energy storage. We recommend therefore, adapting always the
power budget accordingly if the energy budget is increased.
Minimizing the consumed energy budget
The assessed energy consumption of a high-current pulse is defined by the power
and by the time span from changing the programmed current from the quiescent
current to the target current and back to the quiescent current. Slew rate and filter
settings are ignored for the assessment.
For high-current pulses, we recommend therefore, changing the programmed
current to the target value only for the timespan where the higher current is really
required.
Using low slew rates or force filter settings
Slew rate settings and force filter settings are ignored for the calculation of the
required power or consumed energy. The utilization of the budgets is always
calculated from the programmed compliance voltage and the programmed clamp
current (VF mode) or programmed force current (IF mode). This behavior must be
observed when using low slew rates or force filter settings:
Increasing the compliance voltage or the current:
The calculated and assessed energy consumption is higher than the really
required energy. The virtual, channel specific energy storage may be empty
earlier than expected and the related channel will be disconnected.
Decreasing the compliance voltage or the current:
The calculated and assessed energy consumption is lower than the really
required energy. The energy storage of the related eight-channel group may be
empty earlier than expected and all channel of the group will be disconnected.
For use cases in which the low-rated energy of the falling edge is not compensated
by the over-rated energy of the rising edge, we recommend therefore, replacing the

Using the hardware view to clear active flags of an FVI16 in PMU operating mode
The output relays of an FVI16 channel in PMU operating mode may be sometimes
locked without any error message shown and disconnecting and reconnecting all
pins does not change this behavior. The ADC sub-panel of the hardware view must
be used in this case to start a dummy measurement with the relay action set to NT.

FVI16 programming - Stacking
To increase the output voltage, multiple FVI16 channels can be connected in series. This
is called "stacking".
Stacking
Stacked FVI16 channels can be setup under user control or under software control:
User‑controlled stacking:
Maximum three channels are simply connected in series. Setups and measurement
are programmed individually for each of the stacked channels. Measured voltages
must be added together to get the total voltage of the stack. Special setups are
required for forcing current by stacked channels.
Software‑controlled stacking:
The serial connected channels are defined as stacking group in the pin definitions
of SmarTest. The stacking group is accessed as single pin. The on‑board-stacking
controller distributes the total output voltage equally between the stacked
channels. This solution will show a stable output signal and provides reliable
voltage measurements without applying special setups as required for stacking
under user control.
We recommend therefore, always setting up the software‑controlled stacking.
Topic 152726

Stacking characteristics
The following rule applies to both software‑controlled stacking and to stacking under
user control:
Stacking is allowed up to a maximum floating range of ±200 V with respect to the
DUT board ground.
The following items must be considered when using software‑controlled stacking of
FVI16 channels:
Stacking is allowed for any combination of up to three channels within a card.
Stacking is supported only in the high‑power mode. Stacking is not supported in
the high‑voltage mode.
Stacking is not supported for channels that are ganged under software control.
The time measurement unit (TMU) is not supported for software‑controlled
stacking.
The voltage surge tracker is not supported for software‑controlled stacking.
Stacking groups can be disbanded and the individual channels can be assigned
within the same testflow. For more information, refer to FVI16 stacked or ganged
on the fly.

Defining pins
Stacking groups for software‑controlled stacking are defined in the Digital Pins editor.
Therefore, software‑controlled stacking is supported only in the PMU operating mode.
Up to three stacked channels per site can be defined in column Tester Channel of the
Digital Pins editor using the following format:
The stacked channels are to be separated by a semicolon ";".
Single channels must be defined. Grouping by the "-" (hyphen) is not supported.
The first channel on the left defines the uppermost channel that acts as master
channel.
The following channels are the slave channels.
The last channel an the right defines the lowermost slave channel.
CAUTION "Uppermost channel" in this context means the channel that is
connected to the DUT while the "lowermost channel" points towards a stable
reference like ground or the supply voltage of the DUT. This applies also for negative
voltages.
The graphics above shows two stacking groups in rows 3 and 4 of the Digital Pins editor:
Unlike the ganging group in row 2 that uses a comma "," as separator, the stacked
channels must be separated by a semicolon ";". For more information refer to Digital
Pins editor.

Stacking on the fly
"Stacking on the fly" means that a group of stacked channels can be disbanded and the
individual channels can be assigned to other pins of the DUT according to the needs of
the test flow.
Reusing of FVI16 channels requires different connection set definitions. These
connection sets are defined in column Connection Set of the Digital Pins editor.
Therefore, stacking on the fly requires setting up the FVI16 channels in the PMU
operating mode.
For more information on how to set up reused channels, refer to DC Scale pin (PMU
mode) setup.
An FVI16 channel must be disconnected before it can be reused in another stacking
group or as single pin.
Software overview
No special APIs are required to control FVI16 pins using stacked FVI16 channels. The
complete functionality is covered by APIs SPMU_TASK and SPMU_PIN_TASK for an FVI16
in PMU operating mode.
For software controlled stacking, the usable range for forcing, clamping or measuring
voltages is multiplied by the number of stacked channels and the compliance voltage is
to be set accordingly. Depending on the number of stacked channels, the voltage range
is ±120 V or ±180 V. The programmable and usable range of all other settings is not
changed.

Application notes
Stacking on the fly in combination with DC events
For pins that use connection sets, pattern containing DC events must be set up as a
multiport burst. A port can only contain pins with the same connection set or only
pins with the default connection set. The use of a multiport timing is required if
connection sets are defined for the related pins.
For more information regarding the default connection set, refer to Digital Pins
editor and DFPN, DFPN?
Battery level measurements of stacked FVI16 channels
FVI16 features two on‑board energy storages for pulsed high‑current tests that are
assigned to the channel groups 1 … 8 and 9 … 16. Stacking across these two groups
is supported. For stacking groups that cover both channel groups and therefore
utilize both energy storages, the battery level measurement returns the lower of the
two charging levels.
For more information, refer to parameter FVI16_connectionState in
SPMU_PIN_TASK.connectState(), Special events for FVI16 in EVENT_... - DC events API
reference and the SmartRDI function rdi.dc().vMeasBattery().
Discharge before breaking up stacking groups
Using Stacking on the fly in combination with relays on the DUT board allows you
breaking up stacking groups and reusing the stacked channels in other
configurations.
The parasitic capacitance to GND of a reused, previously stacked FVI16 channel
keeps the stacking voltage for a short time. Connecting such a channel immediately
to another DUT pin may damage this pin.
We recommend therefore discharging all channels of a stacking group by forcing 0 V
before breaking up the group.

FVI16 programming - Surge tracker
The FVI16 features a surge tracker per channel that monitors the voltage between the
high sense (HS#) and low sense (LS#) pins or the output current of the PMU. Once the
surge tracker is turned on, it monitors the voltage or current unless being turned off. In
a typical use scenario the surge tracker is activated in the very beginning of a testflow
and the status is checked at the end of the testflow.
API overview

and DPS_AUX_PIN_TASK.

Application notes
TMU and surge tracker
The TMU (Time measurement unit) and the surge tracker cannot be used in parallel.
The two functionalities use the same comparators that can be assigned to only one
of them at the same time.
Surge tracker is silently disabled in temporarily unganged mode
Note that on AVI64, DPS128/64, and FVI16 you cannot execute a current compare on
a ganged group of channels if the group is in unganged mode. Already activated
comparators are silently disabled in unganged mode. A user notification (Error or
warning) is omitted in this case, to avoid any interrupt in the testflow. The previous
state of the comparators is automatically restored after the ganged group has been
restored.
Surge tracker monitors either voltage or current but not both
Although the digital closed loop control of FVI16 channels samples voltage and
current simultaneously, the surge tracker can monitor either the voltage or the
current but not both at the same time.

FVI16 programming - TMU
The FVI16 card features a time measurement unit (TMU) per pin that is available in the
PMU operating mode.
TMU characteristics
The following items must be considered when using the TMU:
The TMU is supported in the PMU operating mode.
The TMU is not supported in the DPS operating mode.
For ganged pins, the time measurement unit (TMU) is supported but only the
high‑speed voltage comparator and the high‑resolution voltage comparator of the
PMU can be used. The measurement is performed on the master channel. The
high‑resolution current comparator of the PMU is not supported.
The default connection set must be used for TMU measurements.
The TMU uses features that are designed for digital pins. Therefore, the DC Scale
specific connection sets cannot be used. TMU measurements can be applied only
on pins defined in the default connection set.
For more information regarding the default connection set refer to Digital Pins
editor and DFPN, DFPN?.
Topic 152734

Basic considerations for programming TMU measurements
The following items should be considered for TMU measurements both using SmartRDI
or TM APIs:
The arm event is the reference for the time stamps.
The arm event is automatically inserted into the pattern burst by SmartRDI and
must be manually inserted for programming by TM API using EVENT_TMU_START.
Time stamps are recorded only after a TMU measure event has been executed in
the pattern.
A measure event is inserted into the pattern by SmartRDI function
rdi.tmu().measMode() or by TM API EVENT_TMU_MEAS.
The basic comparator settings must be applied before the pattern or pattern burst
is started.
Although the related SmartRDI functions can be programmed only in pattern‑based
mode, SmartRDI applies the settings before the pattern burst is started.
For test method API based programming, the related settings must be applied by
the DPS_AUX_PIN_TASK API as shown below.
Measurement filters
FVI16 channels feature programmable anti‑aliasing, low‑pass measurement filters for all
ADCs:
Voltage measurement ADC of the PMU
Current measurement ADC of the PMU
Voltage drop measurements on the force line and on the return line
Battery level measurements at the on-board energy storages
Measurement filter characteristics
Mode Range Measurement filter
Min Max Default
High-power All voltage ranges and all current ranges 100 Hz 250 kHz 250 kHz
High-voltage All current ranges 100 Hz 250 kHz 250 kHz
The dynamic behavior of the force output is independent of the measurement filters.

Note  The high-resolution comparators of the TMU utilize the continuous data
stream of the ADCs. The measurement filter setting has therefore also an effect on
the TMU measurements.
For high-speed TMU measurements using the high-resolution comparators, we
therefore recommend setting the measurement filter to the maximum value.

SmartRDI overview
The complete TMU functionality is covered by the tmu() API of SmartRDI. For more
information refer to SmartRDI: TMU test setup and the related member functions of the
API.
The TMU core functionality is supported only in the pattern‑based mode of SmartRDI.
The code based mode is not supported. We strongly recommend using the
pattern‑based mode with the execution mode set to TA::BURST or TA::PROD. The
mode TA::SINGLE is not recommended for TMU measurements. For more information
refer to RDI_BEGIN().

Application notes
TMU and surge tracker
The TMU (Time measurement unit) and the surge tracker cannot be used in parallel.
The two functionalities use the same comparators that can be assigned to only one
of them at the same time.
Dummy vectors between EVENT_TMU_MEAS and the edge to be measured
Some dummy vectors are required to set up and activate the measurement unit. A
delay time of minimum 100 ns is required between the EVENT_TMU_MEAS and the
first comparator event to be recorded. Comparator events are not recorded and will
be lost if these vectors are omitted.
Number of vectors before pattern end
Due to inter module communication it is required to keep the pattern running for a
short time after the last TMU related DC event. The actual required time depends on
the setup. In case of insufficient number of vectors before pattern stop, a
communication error might occur.
Rules:
Do not specify less than 41 vectors.
60 vectors should work for most of the applications.
If the test execution stops with a communication error, add additional vectors at the
end of the pattern to ensure the error is not caused by an insufficient number of
vectors.
The TMU and the DC event controlled measurements utilize the same path to
transfer data from the front end to the test processor. The combination of the two
kinds of measurements in the same pattern burst on the same pin may increase the
required number of vectors before the pattern end.
TMU and API "waitTMUFinished"
Executing API TMU_PINS.waitTMUfinished() after running the TMU measurement
pattern is mandatory but you cannot rely on the returned status information. The API
TMU_RESULTS.getNumberOfMeasuredSamples() is to be used for checking the
number of valid samples.
The FVI16 TMU is optimized for single shot measurements. The front end will
automatically append eight dummy samples at the end of a measurement to enable
the TMU handling single shot measurements. The dummy samples cannot be
uploaded but are taken into account by API TMU_PINS.waitTMUfinished().
Missing samples

The AVI64 TMU is able to handle up to eight missing samples. If the sample count,
programmed by API TMU_PINS.setNumSamples(), cannot be acquired, the following
behavior will be observed:
1 … 8 samples missing: The captured values can be uploaded.
More than eight samples missing: No values can be uploaded. The API
TMU_RESULTS.getNumberOfMeasuredSamples() will return 0 for the respective
pin and all measurements.
High-resolution current comparators are silently disabled in temporarily unganged
mode
Note that on AVI64, DPS128/64, and FVI16 you cannot execute a current compare on
a ganged group of channels if the group is in unganged mode. Already activated
comparators are silently disabled in unganged mode. A user notification (Error or
warning) is omitted in this case, to avoid any interrupt in the testflow. The previous
state of the comparators is automatically restored after the ganged group has been
restored.

Things to consider during debugging
To minimize thermal effects on measurements the power pulse should be short.
This is also needed to enable power measurements on the wafer.
To enable currents larger than 3 A use pulse mode.
High power tests should be pattern controlled (put into RDI_BEGIN()/RDI_END()).
Compile and run code offline first, to avoid damage by continuous high current
during an error stop of the script.
Run the compiled tests without a DUT first, and check using an oscilloscope that the
signals look as expected.
Keep an eye out for high voltages during debugging, for your safety and the safety
of others.
Do not disconnect the DUT board during debugging. First set down and disconnect
all system resources and open the relays.
CAUTION Do not debug remotely!
High voltages may be present on the DUT board, so you need to see that it
is covered and access is restricted.
Power tests may damage the DUT, so always use an oscilloscope to check
signals first.
Use your eyes and nose to detect if something goes wrong.
Checklist for secure switch-off routine while debugging
At the end of a test program a secure switch-off routine must always be executed.
During debugging, every test suite must have a test to set down higher voltages.
This test must be executed manually by the test engineer in case of run-time errors,
to shut down higher voltages:
1. Set voltage of all power sources to 0 V.
2. Wait a few ms.
3. Disconnect all power sources.
4. Wait a few ms.
5. Disconnect all relays.

FVI16 use case - Connecting and
disconnecting power instrument
Each connection between tester channel and pin of a DUT has at least parasitic
capacitance, parasitic inductivity, and resistance. The stimulation and the measurement
of devices in the power/analog/control sector is done in voltage regions of ±200 V and
in current regions of ±10 A (and more when ganged).
Connecting and disconnecting may be harmful for the DUT, DUT board and power
sensitive tester instruments, if done incorrectly. In the world of power testing, and due
to the huge energy of power instruments, it is necessary to carefully consider the
specific application cases before disconnecting and connecting from/to the DUT or
other electronics.
Topic 349546

Based on specific application scenarios, the software and hardware cannot know what is
happening on the "outside" of the DUT board and they cannot know which future
setting will be needed, before connecting again. Therefore you must carefully plan how
to securely disconnect power channels from external loads and how to connect them in
a safe way to avoid any damage on hardware (DUT, DUT board, tester module).

Sequence for a safe connect:
1. Insert DUT with prober Kelvin contact.
2. Set necessary relay (UTIL/PMUX) connections on the DUT board.
3. Make sure that the 4-wire connection (FORCE and SENSE for HIGH and LOW side)
of power instruments is set correctly.
4. Implement wait time until relays are switched (for example 250 µs for solid state
relays and 1-3 ms for mechanical relays, due to contact bouncing).
5. Use the .preCharge(TA::SAFE_CON) feature for connecting a channel.
6. Consider setting a proper clamp value:
a. Do not set the clamp to the "any" value.
b. For higher current clamp values, the source will reserve more power internally.
c. In case of a short-circuit, the current could be limited to the clamp value.
d. Consider clamp values higher than the given DUT specification-limits
(otherwise current could be limited by clamp and would never fail).
e. Note  Single channels can drain the hopper energy (see FVI16 use case -
Power budget management and power analyst tool) in case of huge power
consumption (for example device has a short to GND). In this case, a
defective device could influence other sites and other sites will fail.
7. For high power pulses, use pattern‑based programming within RDI_BEGIN() /
RDI_END() and the syntax vPulse() or iPulse().
Follow the list below to use the preCharge(TA::SAFE_CON) feature at every connect
sequence:
1. Close relays/PMUX on the DUT board first.
2. Perform a connect of the channel with preCharge(TA::SAFE_CON):
a. The instrument first connects in Hi-Z by closing sense relays only.
b. After a short wait time the instrument measures the voltage level as seen
"outside".
c. The instrument selects the same voltage level as force level.
d. After a short wait time the instrument closes the force relays as well (no hot-
switching, because voltage levels are the same).
e. The instrument will change the force value from the measured value to the
value as selected in the force command.
The process is illustrated in the figure below.

Sequence for a safe disconnect
1. Consider the correct power down sequence for different DUT channels as given in
the DUT spespecification.
2. Reduce force & clamp values:
a. For passive DUT pins: force voltages down to 0 V and discharge the traces and
DUT board capacities.
b. For active DUT pins: reduce current clamp to a minimum and keep the forced
voltage.
3. Wait until capacities/traces are discharged. (You may check this with an
oscilloscope, because the wait time is dependent on current clamps and size of the
capacity.)
4. Execute the .disconnect() command.
5. Open the relay (UTIL/PMUX) connections.
6. Eject device or continue with another relay connection.

FVI16 use case - Switching PMUX and UTIL
while FVI16 is connected
To minimize test time, it can be necessary to switch UTIL/PMUX relays several times
within one pattern run without leaving the pattern. But instruments cannot

Topic 349566

Hot switching
There are different philosophies regarding hot switching:
1. Hot switching means switching relays while source is connected, regardless of the
forced voltage/current value.
2. Hot switching means switching relays while source is connected AND force
voltage/current is over certain limits. In case of setting voltage/current force/clamp
values to a minimum, the switching of relays would no longer be dangerous.
Philosophy 1 would lead to a strict source disconnect / power down, before switching
any relays (UTIL/PMUX). This results in a higher test time due to the additional
instructions, and another pattern start for controlling relays after disconnecting the
source are needed.
For philosophy 2, reduce the forced & clamped voltage/current to a minimum, to avoid
harmful spikes following this approach:
1. Minimize force/clamp values as much as possible, for example vForce(0 V) and
iClamp(100 uA).
2. Use appropriate wait time, for instance for discharging lines/caps.
3. Switch the relays (pattern‑based: sequencer‑controlled / PMUX / routing tool
support).
4. Use appropriate wait time for relay switching, for example 3 ms (mechanical) and
250 µs (PhotoMOS).
5. Increase force/clamp values to target values

General considerations
For a Kelvin connection, force and sense on both the high side and the low side of the
source must be connected at the DUT. While the source is connected, all connections in
the path must be solid and stable.
Instability of that connections could be due to a weak contact of tester pogo pins, the
pogo tower, or the DUT Pad. A wrong connection / wiring on the DUT board or PMUX
relays may also disturb a proper Kelvin connection.
While the FVI16 channel is connected, opening the Kelvin connection would lead to a
disconnect of the source for safety reasons. Therefore make sure that the internal
force/sense link is closed, before any UTIL/PMUX gets switched on the DUT board. After
switching the UTIL/PMUX on the DUT board and after waiting the necessary wait time
(for example 250 µs for solid state relays and 1-3 ms for mechanical relays), the F/S
(Force/Sense) link must be opened again.
See FVI16 use case - Kelvin and 4-wire connection for more details.

Special recommendations for FVI16
We can follow the approach from the Hot switching section, by adding instructions for
enabling and disabling the internal F/S link:
1. Minimize force/clamp values as much as possible for example vForce(0 V) and
iClamp(100 uA).
2. Use appropriate wait time, for instance for discharging lines/caps.
3. Set event to enable internal F/S link.
4. Switch the relays (pattern‑based: sequencer‑controlled / PMUX / routing tool
support) to a new target.
5. Use appropriate wait time for relay switching, for example 3 ms (mechanical) and
250 µs (PhotoMOS).
6. Set event to disable the internal F/S link.
7. Increase force/clamp values to target values.
8. Note  FVI16 will automatically disconnect when force and sense lines of the
force and return path are open. To avoid this automatically triggered
disconnect, set the F/S link event before switching relays, and set the event to
disable the F/S link right after relay switching before continuing testing.

FVI16 use case - Power budget management
and power analyst tool
One FVI16 card has 16 channels. These channels will be supplied by 2 "Hoppers".
Hopper 1 for channels 1-8 and hopper 2 for channels 9-16.
It is necessary to think about how to distribute the requirements to the channels.
A hopper is a container for a bulk material such as grain, typically one that tapers
downwards and is able to discharge its content. In our case, it is capacitance to be
charged, see figures below.
Topic 349570

Example
Eight channels with low power requirements on hopper 1 and eight channels with high
power requirements on hopper 2 can lead to too little energy on hopper 2.
Instead distribute the eight low and the eight high power requirement channels equally
on the two hoppers, which will help for a common discharge, and avoids that one
hopper gets empty.

Programmable Compliance Voltage
The programmable compliance voltage is the raw voltage, which is physically available
for each channel (each Force Amplifier).
All energy which cannot be distributed as output voltage to the DUT generates heat,
which is absorbed by the water cooled heat sink. This absorbed energy may be needed
from other channels that need more energy.
The following example shows the impact of improper selected compliance voltage:
Channel one shows a good selection of compliance voltage at the ratio of the
programmed output voltage.
Channels two to seven shows that the compliance voltage level is selected too high.
There is unused headroom, which may be needed for other channels.
Channel eight shows that the target signal cannot be reached, because there is not
enough headroom available.
Note  Consider programming the appropriate compliance voltage for each channel.

Current force

Voltage force
The voltage will be set in the PMU DAC. The Power Amplifier distributes the
programmed voltage via the high force pogo pins (HF#) to the DUT. The voltage then
flows through the DUT and back to the low force pogo pins (LF#). The force path is
marked with purple in the Block diagram.
Based on the external load and current clamps, high current can flow through the Force
lines. Therefore, consider the trace width in the DUT board design.
Source regulation feedback and voltage Meas
The forced voltage is measured differentially via the two sense lines High Sense (HS#)
and Low Sense (LS#) with the ADC. This measurement is used as source regulation
feedback and for a measurement when performing rdi.dc().vMeas(). The meas/feedback
path is marked with green in the Block diagram.
Note: These pins must be connected via a Kelvin contact together with the respective
Force-pin to the DUT.
Current clamp & current Meas
The programmable current clamp will be measured via the shunt resistor in the HF#
path right after the Force Amplifier. See description in FVI16 use case - SmartRDI - Force
and measure currents.
In parallel to the active current clamp capability, the measured ADC value can be used
for a current measurement when performing rdi.dc().iMeas().

Topic 349741

Fast current clamp
A sudden short between HF# and LF# pins causes high current flow exceeding current
limit settings for a limited time. This is referred to as current spike transients.
The fast current clamp is a circuitry within the FVI16 channel to minimize the current
spike energy by reducing the current and by reducing the spike duration. In a second
stage the control loop reduces current flow to the programmed current clamp settings.
See FVI16 fast current clamp specifications for more information.

FVI16 use case - SmartRDI - Pulsed
operation
Each channel of the FVI16 card can force a current pulse of up to ±10 A in pulsed mode
for a short time of some milliseconds.
The available energy budget of the on-board energy storages, the power dissipation of
the main driver, and a maximum duty cycle must be considered for the high current
pulses.
The pulsed operation is supported for the PMU operating mode. Use the programmable
bandwidth and slew-rate to optimize the dynamic behavior for different types of pulsed
tests and measurements.
Energy storages
The energy for pulses up to ±10 A is provided by two on-board energy storages that are
shared by groups of eight channels. The FVI16 card monitors the energy consumption of
the individual channels and immediately disconnects a channel if the consumed energy
exceeds the assigned energy budget. For more information, see Energy budget.
Power dissipation
The power dissipation of the main driver is calculated from the voltage drop at the main
driver and the current. It therefore depends on the programmable compliance voltage,
the output voltage, and the actual current.
Each FVI16 channel features an on-board monitor that checks the power dissipation of
the main driver. A channel that exceeds the maximum power dissipation will
immediately be disconnected and must be connected again. Therefore, you should
always set the compliance voltage to the minimum possible value. This will also
minimize the stored energy that is consumed.
measVal_v     =  rdi.id("resID_vMeas").getValue();
measVal_fDrop =  rdi.id("resID_fDrop").getValue();
measVal_rDrop =  rdi.id("resID_rDrop").getValue();
Topic 349742

Maximum duty cycle
The consumed energy and the power dissipation at the main driver limit the maximum
duty cycle. The energy storage must be recharged from the available power budget and
the main driver needs some time for cooling down. For more information see Duty cycle
and recharging of the on-board energy storages.

Force filter
Filter settings are used to overcome for things like overshoots that are based on external
loads (DUT board components or DUT). Sudden load changes often requires filter
settings.
The filter settings are used based on the force mode. rdi.dc().vFilter() is used when
vForce() is used, and rdi.dc().iFilter() is used for iForce().
For example while forcing a voltage clamping current rdi.dc().vFilter() is used until the
current clamp is reached. Then rdi.dc().iFilter() is used as long as the current clamp
condition exists.
Based on the current or voltage feedback, the filter will be applied in the force
regulation path, see the block diagram below.
The two block diagrams illustrates the vFilter() and iFilter() respectively.

The diagram below shows signals with different filter settings. The black line illustrates
an overshoot in a signal that is not using a filter setting. The filter of the blue signal is
inadequate and a small overshoot is seen.
Note  Filter settings must be checked with an oscilloscope for each load and each
condition.
The vFilter()/iFilter() defines a current/voltage bandwidth filter that has an effect on the
dynamic behavior of an FVI16 channel that is forcing or clamping the current/voltage.

SlewRate
Filter settings are used to control the reaction speed of your forced signal. The unit for
the slewRate is volts/µs or ampere/µs.
Based on DUT specification requirements, the tester instrument must control the
rising/falling speed of the forcing signal. It can be done with defining and executing a
waveform or simply by selecting the slewRate for the force mode.
The diagram below shows signals with different slewRates, from black (max) to green
(minimum).
Internally in the hardware, the FPGA is calculating the DAC steps based on the force
value and slewRate setting.
Setting an FVI16 channel to a low slew rate results in a noticeable time to ramp up or
down. vSlewRate()/iSlewRate() sets the force voltage/current slew rate in Volts/Ampere
per microsecond respectively.
See FVI16 use case - Block diagrams for block diagrams.

Meas filter control
FVI16 channels feature programmable anti‑aliasing, low‑pass measurement filters, for all
ADCs:
Voltage measurement ADC of the PMU,
current measurement ADC of the PMU,
voltage drop measurements on the force line and on the return line,
battery level measurements at the on-board energy storages.
See the bottom of FVI16 use case - Block diagrams for the block diagram for
measFilter(), and see rdi.dc().measFilter(), FVI16 measure voltages, and FVI16 measure
currents for more details.
Load Cap control
The Load Cap control represents the load capacitance on the DUT board. The parameter
is used to adapt the dynamic behavior of an FVI16 channel to different load capacitors.
This filter has an effect on the dynamic behavior when the regulator is forcing or
clamping the voltage. See FVI16 force and clamp voltages for specifications and
rdi.dc().loadCap() for more details.
Consideration for Slew rate & iClamp
Due to the capacitive load of the DUT board and the DUT, increasing the voltage slew
rate will always result in a higher current while the forced voltage changes. If the higher
current exceeds the programmed clamp current, the effective voltage slew rate is limited
and the Constant current flag / CURRENT_CLAMP alarm might be triggered.
For high voltage slew rates, it is therefore recommended to increase the clamp current
for the time while the forced voltage changes.

General safety precautions

Operation

High-voltage protection system
A combination of electrical and mechanical protection devices shall be used to protect
users from exposure to high voltages. High voltage power supply cards comprise a
safety circuit. This has to be regarded as part of the entire high-voltage protection
system.
The following devices must be used to fulfill the safety requirements:
All parts of the DUT board must be equipped with isolating covers.
All parts of the DUT interface must be equipped with isolating covers.
Isolating covers that can be removed or opened without the use of tools must be
fitted with a safety interlock.
This safety interlock must be used to control the safety circuit on all high voltage
power supply cards installed in the test system.
WARNING A faulty DUT or DUT board may cause high voltages to be applied
to various parts of the DUT board or DUT interface. To protect users from exposure
to high voltages, all parts of the DUT board and DUT interface shall be equipped
with isolating covers.

Power diagram
Operating modes
DPS operating mode: The channel is typically used for DPS applications to supply
the DUT. The channel is basically programmed using DPS primary sets. The
connection modes NORM, UNGANG, PULSE, and HIMP are supported. For more
information, refer to PVI8 in DPS operating mode.
To find a summary of all supported resource parameters in the level file, refer to
DPSPINS resources.
PMU operating mode: The channel is typically used for VI applications. The channel
is basically programmed using test methods and APIs. The connection modes for
normal, fast, and pulsed operation and for high impedance voltage measurements
are supported. For more information, refer to PVI8 in PMU operating mode.
A PVI8 channel can be configured either for the DPS operating mode or for the PMU
operating mode but not for both.
Block diagram

Additional features
A Kelvin test unit is available for each channel. The unit is used to verify that the
force lines and the sense lines are connected together.
A current monitor output for each channel provides a voltage proportional to the
output current.
The on-board safety circuit, in combination with related hardware and cover of the
DUT board, prevents the users from being exposed to hazardous voltages.
Test processor and data analysis features
Setup and measurement sequences are controlled by the test processor.
Several alarm flags are available to indicate irregular operating conditions.
Average values are calculated and stored on-board.
A built-in result analysis is available that checks the measurement data against user
specified test limits.
HV (High-Voltage) protection
The PVI8 card may be connected to low-voltage cards via defective DUTs or
unintentionally closed connections. The card provides enough energy to damage the
low-voltage cards in this case. Therefore, we recommend that you implement a HV
(High-Voltage) protection circuitry on your DUT boards to protect the low-voltage cards.
This will improve the uptime of the test system and the throughput of high-voltage
applications.

PVI8 arbitrary waveform generator (AWG)
A PVI8 pin can be used as an arbitrary waveform generator (AWG), supporting both
voltage and current waveforms. The AWG functionality is controlled by pattern
sequencer DC events.
Topic 144820

A PVI8 channel used in AWG mode is set to the PMU operating mode and programmed
like a standard PMU. The initial values for the forced voltage and the clamp current are
set via the usual commands or APIs. The arbitrary waves are defined by events and test
points, stored into the pattern memory and applied to the PVI8 output by the test
processor.
Both, the force voltage value and the clamp current values can be defined as events and
therefore may be controlled by the AWG functionality.
Refer to PVI8 time measurement, AWG, and digitizer specifications for specification data
of a PVI8 channel in the AWG mode.

The AWG of a PVI8 channel is capable of driving voltage waveforms up to an analog
bandwidth of 50 kHz. An overdrive between 0 dB and about 10 dB must be
programmed for frequencies above 10 kHz.

at the force output of the PVI8 channel.

The resulting output amplitude depends always on the dynamic behavior of the PVI8
channel, the DUT board and the DUT. We strongly recommend verifying the waveform

"Guarding" means that the high force line (HF#) and the high sense line (HS#) are
shielded by a line that carries the same voltage as these two lines. This minimizes the

guard line shields the two output lines from the internal current measurement unit of

PVI8 Kelvin test unit
The PVI8 card features a Kelvin test unit, also known as sense-connection test unit. The
Kelvin test unit is available per channel for the HS# to HF# connection and for the LS# to
LF# connection.
Topic 144770

Kelvin test means that the connection from the force lines to the sense lines on the DUT
board or at the DUT pins is verified with a small test current applied. A PASS/FAIL result
is returned.
The Kelvin test unit applies the small test current to the tested force to sense (FS)
connection and measures the voltage drop between the two lines. The measured
voltage is used as criterion for the pass/fail decision and should be near 0.0 V for a good
FS connection.
The Kelvin test unit is available in the PMU operating mode and in the DPS operating
mode.
Note  The purpose of the Kelvin test unit is to ensure that when the DUT is
contacted, the high-impedance sense line is connected to the force line at the DUT
with a sufficiently low contact resistance. Due to the high input impedance of the
sense line, the fixed threshold of several kilo-Ohms will be sufficiently low.
The Kelvin test unit is the only resource that can perform a reliable sense connection
test with a defined test current applied.
Since connections and hardware on the DUT board can sabotage the test of the
sense connections, we recommend that you check the functionality of the test with
open sense connections. All tested sense connections must fail in this verification.
Some basic data must be considered when using the Kelvin test unit:
The Kelvin test unit is available per channel.
The threshold for the pass/fail decision is about 50 kΩ.
The test current is about 5 µA.
The maximum capacitance between the force lines and the corresponding sense
lines is 5 nF.
The internal 100 kΩ resistor between the force lines and the corresponding sense
lines limits the maximum test voltage of the open connection to about 0.5 V.
The test is done serially for the high sense line and the low sense line.
The floating test current supplies allow a parallel test on all available PVI8 channels.
The test can be performed only in the disconnected state of the selected pins.

Operating principle of the PVI8 Kelvin test unit
The PVI8 Kelvin test unit features two floating 5 µA test current supplies that can be
connected to HF# and HS# or LF# and LS#. The voltage between the two measured lines
can be measured differentially.
The test is divided into two measurements:
HF# to HS#: A floating current source applies a test current to the high sense pin
(HS#) and to the high force pin (HF#). The voltage between the two pins is
measured differentially by the voltage measure unit of the channel.
LF# to LS#: A floating current source applies a test current to the low sense pin
(LS#) and to the low force pin (LF#). The voltage between the two pins is measured
differentially by the voltage measure unit of the channel.
The diagrams above show the operating principle of the floating PVI8 Kelvin test unit.
The path of the test current is marked green. The differential voltage measure paths are
marked red and blue.
The test current can flow only on the marked path from the test current source via the
tested FS connection back to the test current source. Additional circuitry on the DUT
board or internal paths of the DUT has no effect on the test result.

PVI8 safety circuit
The card includes an on-board safety circuit to protect users from exposure to
hazardous voltages.
WARNING Voltages greater than 60 V DC may be present on this card. Refer to
PVI8 safety for more information.
On-board safety circuit
The safety circuit consists of the pogo pins SAFETY_5V and SAFETY_GND and related on-
board hardware. An external control voltage must be applied to the two pins to enable
the card.
The card remains disabled if the control voltage is not applied.
This applies to both force voltage ranges and for all current ranges of the PVI8 channels
regardless of the programmed voltage or current.
Behavior with disabled safety circuit
The card behaves as follows if the control voltage is not applied:
All channels are disconnected.
The unipolar (0.5 V to 80 V) force voltage range is disabled on all channels. The
bipolar ±40 force voltage range is enabled.
The safety line flag is set. For more information refer to DPS power flags - get...()
functions and DPS_AUX_TASK.getSafetyLine().
An error message is shown in the report window and in the console window as
soon as the channel is disconnected the next time.

Behavior with enabled safety circuit
The PVI8 card behaves as follows if the safety circuit is enabled:
The unipolar (0.5 V to 80 V) force voltage range is enabled on all channels that are
already set to this range.
All PVI8 channels remain disconnected until they are connected again.
On-board hardware and required DUT board circuitry
To enable the PVI8 card connect a control voltage of +5.0 V DC from an adequate power
supply to the pogo pins SAFETY_5V and SAFETY_GND. The supply must be applied via a
safety interlock that is open when the DUT board cover or the DUT interface cover is
open.
The user-accessible part of the safety circuit is isolated from the rest of the card; thereby
the parallel connection of two or more cards is supported. Refer to PVI8 safety pogo
pins for information on the characteristics of the pogo pins.
Application note
Using the 80 V range after the safety circuit has been toggled
In case the safety line will be opened and closed again while the PVI8 is
disconnected but the test program is already loaded, the PVI8 can only proceed in
the 40 V range. This behavior may be occur if the DUT board is changed with the test
program already loaded.
In this case, you must unlocked the supply by executing a setup or measurement in
the 40 V range and disconnecting the supply again. After that, you can proceed in
the originally selected 80 V range.

PVI8 surge tracker
The PVI8 provides a surge tracker that monitors the voltage between the high sense
(HS#) and low sense (LS#) inputs.
Once the surge tracker is turned on, it monitors the voltage unless being turned off. In a
typical use scenario the surge tracker is activated in the very beginning of a test flow
and the status is checked at the end of the test flow.
The surge tracker checks against both high (positive) and low (negative) voltage
thresholds, which can be set individually. Two flags indicate if thresholds have been
exceeded. These flags are latched (stored) and can be retrieved any time in the test flow.
Please refer to PVI8 other performance specifications for specification data of the surge
tracker.
Application notes
TMU and surge tracker
The TMU (Time measurement unit) and the surge tracker cannot be used in parallel.
The two functionalities use the same comparator set that can be assigned to only
one of them at the same time.
Surge tracker and HIMP mode
When using PVI8 in high impedance (HIMP) measurement mode, the surge tracker is
silently disabled. A user notification (Error or warning) is omitted, to avoid any
interrupt in the test flow. The old status of the surge tracker is automatically restored
if another measurement mode is selected.

PVI8 time measurement unit (TMU)
PVI8 channels in the PMU operating mode feature a high-voltage time measurement
unit (TMU), each providing a high-impedance and a high-bandwidth connection mode.
Topic 144817
Topic 143949

TMU characteristics
The following items must be considered when using the TMU:
The TMU is supported in the PMU operating mode.
The TMU is not supported in the DPS operating mode.
The TMU is not supported for pins ganged under software control.
The default connection set must be used for TMU measurements.
The TMU uses features that are designed for digital pins. Therefore, the DC Scale
specific connection sets cannot be used. TMU measurements can be applied only
on pins defined in the default connection set.
For more information regarding the default connection set refer to Digital Pins
editor and DFPN, DFPN?.
TMU input lines
The TMU uses a differential input that consists of the two pogo pins TMU_H# and
TMU_L#. These pins must be additionally connected to the DUT if the TMU is to be used.
Internal connections from the channel output to the TMU lines are not available.
The pogo pin TMU_L# is a high-speed ground sense pin. The voltage at this pin must be
within a range of ±5 V of the low force (LF#) output of the channel.
TMU connection modes
The TMU provides two connection modes:
High bandwidth connection mode: This range provides a high bandwidth of 30
MHz. The input impedance of both TMU pogo pins is 10 kΩ. The input voltage
range is -40 V to +40 V.
High impedance connection mode: This range provides a bandwidth of 3 MHz. The
input impedance of both TMU pogo pins is 100 kΩ. The input voltage range is -80
V to +80 V.

PVI8 operating modes
The PVI8 card supports the DPS operating mode and the PMU operating mode.
The combination of the operating mode and the selected connection state define the
characteristics, the dynamic behavior, and the basic programming mode of the channels.
The PVI8 operating mode is defined by the pin type that has been selected in the Pin
setting editors. The operating mode can be set individually for each channel of the card.
The connection state is set by additional parameters or APIs.
DPS operating mode
A PVI8 channel is configured to operate in DPS mode if it is defined as a device power
supply using the DPS Pins editor. In DPS mode, the channel behaves like a DPS-slot
device power supply and is normally used to supply devices with power during the
execution of a test flow. A PVI8 channel in DPS operating mode takes part in the
standard connect and disconnect sequences and is programmed using DPS primary
sets.
PMU operating mode
A PVI8 channel is configured for the PMU operating mode if the channel is defined as
DC Scale pin using the Digital Pins editor. In PMU operating mode, the channel is used
like a standard PMU to temporarily supply power during the execution of a single test
suite or a group of test suites. A PVI8 channel in PMU operating mode is programmed
using test methods and APIs.
Supported features in DPS operating mode and PMU
operating mode
Most of the PVI8 features are supported in the DPS operating mode and in the PMU
operating mode but some features are supported only in the PMU operating mode.
The following features are supported only in the PMU operating mode:
The connection state "FAST" that can be set using SPMU_PIN_TASK.connectState()
The ganging on the fly
The time measurement unit (TMU)

PVI8 in DPS operating mode
In DPS mode, a channel behaves like a DPS-slot device power supply and is used to
supply devices with power during the execution of a test flow.
To find a summary of all supported resource parameters in the level file, refer to
DPSPINS resources.
Configuration
A PVI8 channel is configured to operate in DPS mode if it is defined as a device power
supply using the DPS Pins editor.
Characteristics
The channel is typically used for DPS applications to supply the DUT. The channel
provides a positive or negative voltage up to the programmed clamp current and is
programmed using DPS primary sets. Programming a PVI8 channel by DC events is also
supported. The static and dynamic behavior is defined by the connection state as
explained below.
Topic 143878

Connection state
The connection state defines the behavior of the channel in the DPS operating mode.
The following connection states are supported:
norm: The channel is typically used for DPS applications to supply the DUT. The
channel provides a positive or negative static voltage and is able to drive a wide
range of DUT capacitances. The maximum static current per channel is ±1.0 A. The
maximum pulsed current per channel is ±10.0 A. The energy for current pulses
greater than 1.0 A is provided by on-board energy storage. A minimum and a
maximum pulse-width and a maximum duty cycle must be considered for these
current pulses. Current measurements may be performed in all supported
combinations of clamp current ranges and current measure ranges.
ungang: This connection state provides features similar to the norm state, but
ganged slave channels will be temporarily disconnected to improve the accuracy of
low-current measurements.
pulse: This connection state provides features similar to the norm state but the
bandwidth of the channel is higher and the reaction time shorter. The ability to
drive DUT capacitances has been reduced. Forcing, clamping, and measuring of the
output current are limited to the ±10.0 A range. The lower current ranges are not
supported.
himp: The channel is typically used for high impedance differential voltage
measurements. The voltage is measured differentially between the HS# pogo pin
and the LS# pogo pin. The force output switch is open but the force voltage value
must be set to minimize the leakage current through the open switch and to fit to
the requirements of the lower two voltage measurement ranges.
Refer to the PVI8 programming - DPS operating mode for the information how to set
the connection state.

Connecting and disconnecting channels in DPS operating
mode
A PVI8 channel behaves like a DPS-slot device power supply when connecting and
disconnecting channels in DPS operating mode.
When connected, the channel forces the programmed voltage. The current is limited to
the programmed clamp current.
A PVI8 channel must be disconnected before changing any of the following:
The force voltage range.
The clamp current range.
If the DC Scale card is still connected, you cannot activate a DPS set that contains one of
above changes. To avoid damages to your device or the DUT board, the system will
display an error message in the report window instead.

PVI8 in PMU operating mode
In PMU operating mode, a pin is used like a standard PMU to temporarily supply power
during the execution of a single test suite or a group of test suites.
Configuration
A PVI8 channel is configured for the PMU operating mode if the channel is defined as a
DC Scale pin using the Digital Pins editor.
Topic 143879

Characteristics
The channel is typically used for VI applications. The channel provides a positive or
negative voltage up to the programmed clamp current and is programmed using test
methods and APIs.
The static and dynamic behavior and the measurement mode are defined by a
combination of the connection state, the measurement mode, and the execution mode
as described below. Please refer to the PVI8 programming - PMU operating mode.
Connection state
The connection state defines the dynamic behavior of the channel when it is configured
for the PMU operating mode. Please refer to SPMU_PIN_TASK.connectState().
The following connection states are supported:
"NORMAL": The channel is typically used for DPS applications to supply the DUT. The
channel provides a positive or negative static voltage and is able to drive a wide
range of DUT capacitances. The maximum static current per channel is ±1.0 A. The
maximum pulsed current per channel is ±10.0 A. The energy for current pulses
greater than 1.0 A is provided by on-board energy storage. A minimum and a
maximum pulse-width and a maximum duty cycle must be considered for these
current pulses. Current measurements may be performed in all supported
combinations of clamp current ranges and current measure ranges.
"FAST": The channel is typically used for VI applications (for example RDS on). This
connection state provides basically the same features as the Normal state, but the
dynamic behavior is changed. This connection state provides higher bandwidth and
a shorter reaction time but the ability to drive DUT capacitances has been reduced.
"PULSE": This connection state provides features similar to the Fast state, but the
bandwidth of the channel is higher and the reaction time shorter. The ability to
drive DUT capacitances has been reduced. Forcing, clamping, and measuring of the
output current are limited to the ±10.0 A range. The lower current ranges are not
supported.

Measurement mode
The measurement mode defines the force mode and the measurement mode of the
channel when it is configured for the PMU operating mode. Please refer to
SPMU_PIN_TASK.mode().
"IFVM": Force current and measure voltage.
"VFIM": Force voltage and measure current.
"VM_HIZ": The channel is used for high-impedance differential voltage
measurements. The voltage is measured differentially between the HS# pogo pin
and the LS# pogo pin. The force output switch is open but the force voltage value
must be set to minimize the leakage current through the open switch and to stay
within the requirements of the ±1 V and ±5 V voltage measure ranges.
"VFIM_UNGANGED": This measurement mode corresponds to the "SER" and "PAR"
execution modes as described below. However, in this mode ganged slave channels
are temporarily unganged and the measurement is performed only on the master
channel to improve the accuracy of low-current measurements. For voltage
measurements, there is no difference to the "SER" and "PAR" execution modes.
Execution mode
The execution mode defines the measurement behavior of the channel when it is
configured for the PMU operating mode. Please refer to SPMU_PIN_TASK.execMode().
The following execution modes are supported:
"SER": Serial measurements are performed per device, but in multisite tests
multiple sites are tested in parallel whenever possible.
"PAR": Parallel measurements are performed per device and on all sites whenever
possible.

PVI8 force and measure voltages
The PVI8 card features a PMU per channel for forcing and measuring voltages. The
PMUs provide two force voltage ranges and four voltage measurement ranges.
Forcing voltage
The PVI8 channels are linear regulated voltage supplies with remote sense lines. The
voltage controllers of the channels will adjust the forced voltage so that the voltage
between the high sense pogo pin (HS#) and the low sense pogo pin (LS#) is equal to the
programmed voltage as long as the output current stays below the programmed clamp
current.
The card provides two force voltage ranges:
The bipolar force voltage range provides an output voltage from -40.0 V to +40.0 V.
The unipolar force voltage range provides an output voltage from 0.5 V to 80.0 V.
Both force voltage ranges use the same driver and force voltage DACs. The two different
ranges are achieved by moving the low reference pogo pin and return path from the
center ground of the floating supplies to the negative supply voltage of the main driver
as shown in the example below. The reference point of the output voltage is always the
low sense pogo pin (LS#).
The programmed voltage is applied through a filter function.
Topic 143787

Measuring voltage
The voltage is measured differentially between the high sense pogo pin (HS#) and the
low sense pogo pin (LS#). The differential value is used as a voltage feedback value for
the force voltage controller and is used as the input for the voltmeter of the channel.
The voltmeter provides four voltage measurement ranges. The reference point of the
measurements is always the low sense pogo pin (LS#).
High-impedance voltage measurement mode (HIMP)
A high-impedance operation mode is available. This mode is used to measure the
voltage with no voltage or current applied. The force output is switched to a high-
impedance mode. The voltage is measured differentially between the high sense pogo
pin (HS#) and the low sense pogo pin (LS#).
Example
The diagram above shows an example for the two force voltage ranges. The LF# and LS#
pins of both channels are connected to the same DUT pin - usually the reference ground
of the DUT. The upper channel is set to force +0.5 to +80.0 V at the upper DUT pin. The
lower channel is set to force a voltage between -40.0 V and +40.0 V in the bipolar force
voltage range.

PVI8 force voltages
The PVI8 channels are linear regulated power supplies with remote sense lines and two
force voltage ranges. Filters are available to limit the rise and fall times.
Force voltage ranges
The card provides two force voltage ranges:
The bipolar force voltage range provides an output voltage from -40.0 V to +40.0 V.
The unipolar force voltage range provides an output voltage from 0.5 V to 80.0 V.
For the maximum current related to the voltage, refer to PVI8 power diagram and
pulsed current mode specifications.
Switching into and out of the 80 V range requires for a single channel minimum 100 ms
to about 150 ms wait time for internal discharge. Changing the force voltage range of
more than one channel requires minimum 140 ms to about 225 ms. The wait time
depends on the number of changed channels and the programmed force voltage in the
new range.
A PVI8 channel must be disconnected to change the force voltage range.
Dynamic behavior
The programmed voltage is applied through a filter. Selectable filters are:
None (Bypass)
1 Hz to 20 kHz
The load step response depends on the selected current range, on the impedance of the
high force and low force traces on the DUT board, and on the capacitive load on the
DUT board.
Topic 143791

Voltage sense lines
The forced voltage is sensed differentially between the HS# pogo pin and the LS# pogo
pin. These pins must be connected to the HF# pogo pin and to the LF# pogo pin on the
DUT board. The voltage difference between HF# and HS# or between LF# and LS# must
not exceed 5 V. The voltage difference between the force pins and sense pins is typically
caused by voltage drop produced by current flow over parasitic resistances on the DUT
board. Violating this rule will result in a wrong force voltage.

PVI8 measure voltages
The PVI8 card provides a voltmeter that measures the voltage differentially between the
HS# pogo pin and the LS# pogo pin.
The card provides one ADC per channel that is used for voltage and current
measurements. The ADC supports multiple measurements per trigger. The average value
is calculated on the board.
Voltage measurement ranges
Each channel provides the following voltage measurement ranges.
±1 V
±5 V
±40 V
0.5 V ... 80 V
The voltages are measured differentially between the HS# and LS# pogo pins. The
reference point of the measurements is always the low sense pogo pin (LS#).
Topic 143789

Rules for the ±1 V and ±5 V voltage measurement ranges
Some additional rules must be respected for the ±1 V and ±5 V voltage measurement
ranges:
The maximum voltage difference from the HS# or LS# pogo pins to the voltage at
the HF# pogo pin is ±5 V.
The maximum differential voltage between the HS# and the LS# pogo pins is ±5 V.
The high-impedance voltage measurement mode is supported for these two
voltage measure ranges. The force voltage must be set to a value that fulfills the
requirements of the first rule although the high force output is disabled in this
mode.
An input current of up to 4 mA must be expected, and the measurement will be invalid if
the rules are not respected.

PVI8 force, clamp, and measure currents
The PVI8 card provides three clamp current (or force current) ranges and five current
measurement ranges. Guard lines are available to minimize the parasitic leakage
currents on the DUT board.
Force and clamp current
The PVI8 card channels are floating voltage supplies with programmable clamp currents.
These clamp currents can be programmed separately for sourcing and sinking currents.
Currents are forced using the clamp current functionality. The programmed clamp
current is set to the required force current value. The forced voltage must be set above
or below the expected voltage to force the used channel into the clamp current
situation. Setting the force voltage according to the desired current forces the channel
into the clamping situation:
The channel will apply a programmed positive clamp current as long as the actual
voltage is above the programmed voltage.
The channel will apply a programmed negative clamp current as long as the actual
voltage is below the programmed voltage.
The clamp circuitry is connected to the voltage controller of the channel. Dynamic
current changes will not immediately be limited. A short response time until the current
is clamped to the programmed value has to be expected during transitions.
 Minimum 64 samples are used for current measurements in the 50 uA range.
 The ADC sample frequency is the frequency that is valid only for the hardware based
on-board averaging. The ADC sample frequency is to be considered only for calculating
the required sampling time per averaged value. A lower maximum sample frequency,
which is defined in the PVI8 time measurement, AWG, and digitizer specifications, is to
be considered for the sampling rate in pattern.

Topic 143788

Current measurements
Five different ranges are available to measure the actual current on the high force
output line. The hardware is partially shared with the clamp current functionality.
Guard line
One guard line is available for the two output lines HF# and HS# of each channel. This
guard line carries the same voltage as the two output lines and is used to minimize the
parasitic leakage current to the DUT board ground or other lines. For more information
refer to PVI8 guard.

PVI8 measure currents
The PVI8 card provides five different current measurement ranges.
The card provides one ADC per channel that is used for voltage and current
measurements. The ADC supports multiple measurements per trigger. The average value
is calculated on the board.
Current measurement ranges
The card provides five current measurement ranges which can be set individually for
each channel:
±10 A
±300 mA
±20 mA
±1 mA
±50 µA
Topic 143790

Clamp current range and current measurement range
combination
The on-board current measure hardware is partially shared with the clamp current
functionality. Not all combinations of clamp current ranges and current measurement
ranges are supported.
The current measure shunt resistors are divided into two groups:
±10 A range: Two dedicated shunt resistors for the 10 A range are located directly
in the main driver as shown in the block diagram in PVI8 functionality and features.
The main driver and the clamp circuitry use these shunt resistors permanently to
limit the maximum power dissipation and output current of the driver.
±50 µA ... ±300 mA range: Four multiplexed shunt resistors are available for the
lower current ranges. These shunt resistors are located between the main driver
output and the HF# pin as shown in the block diagram. An additional bypass relay
is closed in case current measurements are performed in the ±10 A range.
The clamp current circuitry may be connected to the signal from the ±10 A shunt
resistors or to the multiplexed shunt resistors for the ±300 mA range or the ±20 mA
range.
The current measure circuitry may be connected to the signal from the ±10 A shunt
resistors or to any of the other four multiplexed shunt resistors.
The current measure shunts for the ±300 mA range or ±20 mA are common for the
force (or clamp) range and the measurement range. This results in the limitation that the
current measurement range must be equal to the force current range in case the ±300
mA or ±20 mA force current range has been selected.
No limitations must be considered in case the ±10 A force current range has been
selected. The dedicated shunt resistors for this range may be combined with any of the
other four shunt resistors or the bypass relay can be closed to perform measurements in
the ±10 A range.

PVI8 stacked, ganged, or in pulsed operation
Multiple PVI8 channels can be combined by stacking or ganging to get a higher voltage
or a higher current. The PVI8 channels feature also a pulse operation mode for
generating high-current pulses.
Stacking
In order to achieve a higher output voltage, serial connection of multiple PVI8 channels
is allowed. This is called "stacking". For more information, refer to PVI8 stacked.
Ganging
In order to achieve a higher output current, parallel connection of multiple PVI8
channels is supported. This is called "ganging". For more information, refer to PVI8
ganged.
Ganging on the fly
The floating high-current channels of the card are a limited resource and must be
multiplexed to different DUT pins in most applications. This is normally done via
additional relay multiplexers on the DUT board. "Ganging on the fly" means that the
group of ganged channels can be disbanded and the individual channels can be
assigned to other pins of the DUT according to the needs of the test flow. For more
information, refer to PVI8 ganged on the fly.
Pulsed operation
Each channel of the card is able to force a multiple of the continuous current in pulsed
operation. The energy for such a high current pulse is provided by on-board energy
storages. For more information, refer to PVI8 pulsed operation.

PVI8 stacked
To increase the output voltage, multiple PVI8 channels can be serially connected. This is
called "stacking".
Stacking
All channels of a PVI8 card are fully floating, meaning that the channels feature
individual return pins (LF#) and behave like batteries. The return pins can be connected
to DUT ground or any bias voltage that may also be provided by another PVI8 channel.
Stacking channels requires no additional internal resources or specific software support.
The related channels are programmed like single ground referenced channels. The
required wiring must be set up on the DUT board.
Stacking characteristics
The following items must be considered when stacking PVI8 channels:
Stacking is allowed for two unganged channels or two ganging groups within a
card or across cards.
Stacking is allowed up to a maximum output voltage of ±160 V with respect to the
DUT board ground.
Stacking is allowed both in the bipolar (±40 V) force voltage range and in the
unipolar (0.5 ... 80 V) force voltage range.
DUT board connections
The following connections are required for a stack of two channels:
The high force (HF#) pin and the high sense (HS#) pin of the upper channel must be
connected together at the DUT.
The low force (LF#) pin and the low sense (LS#) pin of lower channel must be
connected together at the DUT.
Low force and low sense of the upper channel and high force and high sense of the
lower channel are to be connected together at a star point.
All of the required DUT board connections may be routed via optional relay
multiplexers.
