__data__.text:
State setup
"State Name" column
The name of the states is defined in the State Name column. The states are
referenced by this name when they are selected and applied by the related SmartRDI
functions.
The names of the states must be unique for the complete table. Supported
characters are:
Alphanumeric characters A ... Z, a ... z, and 0 ... 9
Blank character, hyphen, underscore, and dot.
"Master File Link" column
If an XML file is defined in this column, the Routing Tools master file is used and the
corresponding routing state is outsourced to the defined slave file.
"Switch Mode" column
The Switch mode defines how the routing states are applied by SmartRDI. The
following values are supported:
BBM: The "Break Before Make" mode means that switch states "0" are applied
first:
1. All switch states "0" are applied.
2. The Off Wait [ms] settling time is applied if switches have been changed in
step 1.
3. All switch states "1" are applied.
4. The On Wait [ms] settling time is applied if switches have been changed in
step 3.
The purpose of this mode is to avoid short circuits between DUT pins or tester
resources. A short time where all changed connections are in switch state "0"
must be considered for the DUT and the used resources. This mode needs a
little more test time for applying the data in two steps and the additional wait
time as defined in column Off Wait [ms].
MBB: The "Make Before Break" mode means that switch states "1" are applied
first:
1. All switch states "1" are applied.
2. The On Wait [ms] settling is applied if switches have been changed in step
2.
3. The switch states "0" are applied.

metadata.file_name: SmartRDI_ DUT board connections control by Routing Tools.pdf
metadata.file_path: C:\Users\shuklajiwank\Documents\sendihack\SmartRDI_ DUT board connections control by Routing Tools.pdf

metadata.file_name: SmartRDI_ DUT board connections control by Routing Tools.pdf
metadata.file_path: C:\Users\shuklajiwank\Documents\sendihack\SmartRDI_ DUT board connections control by Routing Tools.pdf

__data__.text:
4. The Off Wait [ms] settling is applied if switches have been changed in step
3.
The purpose of this mode is to avoid undefined connections between DUT pins
and tester resources. A short time where all changed connections are in switch
state "0" must be considered for the DUT and the used resources. This mode
needs a little more test time for applying the data in two steps and the
additional wait time as defined in column On Wait [ms].
IMM: The "Immediate mode" means that the routing state is applied
immediately in one step for all utility pins and PMUX pins:
1. All switch state "0" and "1" are applied.
2. The IMM Wait [ms] is applied if switches have been changed in step 3.
This mode requires no additional test time but the overlapped switching
behavior is not defined.
"Off Wait [ms]" column
The wait time to be applied after switches are changed from closed state to open
state can be defined in this column. The value is to be defined in milliseconds [ms].
Fractional numbers are supported. For more information refer to the description of
the switch modes above.
"On wait [ms]" column
The wait time to be applied after switches are changed from open state to closed
state can be defined in this column. The value is to be defined in milliseconds [ms].
Fractional numbers are supported. For more information refer to the description of
the switch modes above.
"IMM Wait [ms]" column
The wait time to be applied for switch mode IMM can be defined in this column. The
value is to be defined in milliseconds [ms]. Fractional numbers are supported.
"Hybrid state" column
An exclamation mark points the user to a state which is mixing static utility lines and
sequencer‑controlled utility lines or sequencer‑controlled PMUX switches.
You should avoid mixing the static access of utility lines with sequencer control of
utility lines or PMUX switches since pattern burst of SmartRDI are interrupted to
switch static utility lines in between. The result of mixing is a bad test time and
inhomogeneous switching sequences, especially in context with BBM and MBB
switch modes.
"Execution" row - Switch Mode and wait times

__data__.text:
The default values for the Switch mode, the Off Wait [ms], the On Wait [ms], and
the IMM Wait [ms] are defined in the four cells of row Execution. These values are
applied if no values are defined in the routing state rows below.
State definition table
The state definition table on the right side contains the switch states for all routing
states of all configured pins.
The header row shows the names of all utility pins and all PMUX pins that have been
defined in the Utility Lines Config editor and in the PMUX Config editor.
The next row shows the type of the resource:
S: Static utility line
D: Dynamic utility line
P: PMUX channel
The following rows contain the switch states per routing state that are assigned to
the configured pins.
The switch states to be applied are defined for each stored state and for all utility
pins and PMUX pins. The following switch states are supported:
0: The channel is inactive:
Utility line low‑side switch to UGND is open
PMUX switch is open
1: The channel is active:
Utility line low‑side switch to UGND is closed
PMUX switch is closed
X: The utility pin or the switch is not changed.
Note that when adding a new routing state or pin, the cells of the new row or
column are filled with "." and highlighted in red to mark these initial settings as
invalid.

Other controls and tasks
Filter column and row
The filter column and filter row are highlighted light-blue. You can enter your filter

The filter for the state setup table supports a logical OR expression using the vertical
bar "|": Enter 0|1 to show only columns containing "0" or "1".
Toolbar
The State Setup editor features a toolbar that helps you setting the states.
The toolbar provides these features:
Highlight all "0", "X" or "1"

__data__.text:
State setup table
The state setup table shows the actual state of all switches and utility lines and allows
you interactively modifying all settings.
CAUTION The settings of the switches and utility lines are immediately applied
to the hardware as soon as you modify a value and leave the modified cell.
The table is divided into two sections:
All_Sites row: The uppermost row shows the common state for all sites. Settings
that are different for the sites are shown as question mark "?". Modifications in the
uppermost row are applied to all sites.
Site_# rows: These rows show the state per site. A modification in one of these rows
is applied only to the related site.
The current edit position in the table highlighted orange in the sites column and in the
header row. The light-blue row and column allow you entering filters for the rows and
columns.
The shown switch states are defined as follows:
0: The channel is inactive:
Utility line open collector output is off
PMUX switch is open
1: The channel is active:
Utility line open collector output is on
PMUX switch is closed
?: The actual state is different on the sites. This switch is used only in the uppermost
All_Sites row.
Note  The state setup table shows the current state of the hardware. The switch
state X (do not change) of the State Setup editor is therefore not supported.
State drop-down list and "Apply" button
The routing states that have been defined using the State Setup editor can be selected
from the State drop-down list and applied to the hardware by clicking the Apply
button.

__data__.text:
Procedure
1. Define the digital control pins.
Digital control pins must be defined for controlling utility lines by the pattern
sequencer and for generating the signals for the IC interface of MUX cards.
a. Identify the digital control pins for utility pogo blocks and MUX cards that are
wired on the DUT board.
b. Define minimum three digital pins for the signals FRAMn, SCLK, and SINP per
utility line control group. For more information refer to Sequencer-controlled
utility lines - Serial interface.
c. Enter the two digital pins per MUX card control group. For more information
refer to PMUX01 I2C interface.
2. Load or create an XML file and enter the global configuration data.
The XML file holds the complete configuration data for the Routing Tools.
a. Select the Global Setup editor tab.
b. Create a new XML file or select an existing XML file using the File Path field or
the Browse... button. The file extension ".xml", ".zip" or ".rtz" defines whether
the file to load is a text file or a compressed file.
c. Click the Load button for loading the selected file.
d. Enter the number of configured sites in field Site Number. The number of
configured sites must be the same as defined by the Define Site Number
dialog of SmarTest. For more information refer to Defining additional test sites.
e. Select the type of utility pogo blocks in field Pogo block size.... The selected
value must be the same as defined as parameter
utility_lines_per_pogoblock in the .technology file of the device. For
more information refer to Technology file for a device.
f. If sequencer‑controlled utility lines are used enter a clock frequency in field SPI
Max. Clock Rate. The maximum supported clock frequency is defined in
Sequencer-controlled utility lines - Specifications.
g. Define the behavior of MUX card switches for failing sites and enter the clock
frequency in field I2C Max. Clock Rate. A standard multiple like " MHz" may
be added to the value typed in. The maximum clock frequency must not
exceed "1 MHz". For more information refer to PMUX01 I2C interface.
3. Define the control data for utility lines.
2

The operating mode of the utility pogo blocks and the assignment of the digital
control pins for sequencer‑controlled utility lines need to be defined.
a. Select the Utility Lines Control editor tab.
b. Use the Control Table for defining the operating mode for each of the used
utility blocks.
c. Use the Pin Config Table for defining the digital control pins if
sequencer‑controlled utility lines are used. The selected digital pins must
already be defined in the Digital Pins editor. On the DUT board, the selected
pins must be wired to the serial interface for sequencer controlled utility lines.
4. Define the configuration data for utility lines.
The assignment from tester channels or utility pogo pins respectively to user
defined utility pin names is done in this step.
a. Open the SmarTest Utility Pins editor.
b. Define all required utility pin names and assign them to the tester channels
UTI## ... UTI## for all configured sites.
c. Select the Utility Lines Config editor tab of the Routing Tools.
d. Copy all names and tester channels from the Utility Pins editor to the
corresponding cells of the Utility Lines Config editor tab. The names defined in
this tab and the names defined in the PMUX Config editor tab must be unique
for the complete XML configuration file. The utility pins that are defined in this
step must be the same as defined in the Name column of the Utility Pins
editor.
5. Define the control data for MUX cards.
MUX cards are controlled via an IC interface. Digital pins, which generate the IC
signals, are selected and configured in this step.
a. Select the PMUX Control editor tab.
b. Identify the MUX cards and the related pogo blocks in the circuit diagram of
the DUT board.
c. Type in the MUX card addresses in column Module ID and select the
appropriate Control Group. MUX card addresses are defined by the state of
the four pogo pins ID0 ... ID3 and are normally hardwired on the DUT board.
For more information refer to MUX cards pogo block numbering, PMUX01
programming interface and to PMUX01 addressing scheme.

a. Select the PMUX Config editor tab.
b. Type in the user defined PMUX pin names in column Name. The name defined

7. Define the routing states.
The routing states to be applied to utility lines and PMUX channels are defined in

b. Select the default switch mode and enter the default wait times in milliseconds

c. Enter the user defined routing state name in column State Name.

Break), or IMM (Immediate mode) in column Switch Mode if the value defined

__data__.text:
The routing states to be applied are defined in the State Setup editor and stored in an
XML file that is defined and has been loaded in the Global Setup editor. In order to
enable collaboration when defining the routing states, selected routing states can be
outsourced to one or more slave files and can be edited and extended independently of
each other in theses slave files.
Files handled when using a master file
When a master file is used, multiple files are handled by the Routing Tools editors:
Master file
The master file is a pure text file and uses the file extension ".mfh". It is
generated when routing states are outsourced to separate XML files. The master
file references the original XML file and all slave files. When loaded in the Global
Setup editor, the State Setup editor shows the routing states stored in the
original XML file and the outsourced routing states of all used slave files.
Original XML file
This file contains all routing states that are not outsourced and is also the
master file for all other settings defined in the other tabs. These are the global
settings, the utility line control and configuration settings, and the MUX card
control and configuration settings.
For a smooth collaboration, the global settings as well as the control and
configuration settings should be available before defining and outsourcing
routing states. These settings can also be changed later, but may require rework
in the slave files.
Slave files
Slave files contain outsourced routing states. The files are referenced in the
master file. All routing states of the slave files and the routing states left in the
original XML file are shown in the State Setup editor if a master file is loaded.
A slave file contains also a copy of the global settings and the control and
configuration data of the original XML file and can therefore be loaded
independently from the other files to edit or add routing states.
Rules
Some rules must be observed when using a master file:
Once a master file has been generated, the master file must be loaded if
other routing states are to be outsourced, or
global settings and the control and configuration data need to be changed,
or

Routing states must first be marked as outsourced by inserting the name of a slave file
so that when saving the setup, a master file can be created or updated and the routing
states can be moved from the original XML file into slave files.
After that, the outsourced states can be edited in the slave files and merged back into
the original XML file.
It is also possible to import an existing routing setup file into another routing setup file.
Outsourcing routing states and creating a master file
Routing states that should be outsourced to a slave file must first be marked in the
State Setup editor. When saving, a new master file is created if required, and the
marked routing states are moved to the slave files.
Outsourcing routing states
Routing states can be outsourced to separate XML files by entering a file name in
the "Master File Link" column of the State setup editor.
Some rules to consider:
Outsourcing is supported for multiple routing states and multiple slave files
can be used.
A slave file can contain multiple routing states but an outsourced routing
state can exist only in one slave file. The decisive factor here is the name of

File name of the slave files:
The file name must be defined with the extension ".xml" in lowercase
letters.
The file path can be absolute or relative to the currently loaded XML file
or master file.
Regardless of how the file path is defined, it is always stored as an
absolute path. The absolute path is shown in a tool tip when you hover
the mouse pointer over the entry.
The editor immediately moves outsourced routing states to the end of the
table.
Changes are finally accepted only when the setup is saved.
Some hints regarding the handling of the slave files:
If no master file is loaded, a slave file will be created if it does not exists.
If a master file already has been loaded, a slave file that is already in use is
extended by a newly outsourced routing state.
An already existing slave file that was not previously referenced in the
master file is overwritten with the newly outsourced routing states.
Saving the set up
The changes in the State Setup editor must be saved so that a master file can be
created or updated and outsourced routing states can be moved to the slave
files:
If a master file is already loaded, it will be updated with new slave files. The
routing states to be outsourced are moved from the original XML file to
existing or newly created slave files.

file opens:

Enter the desired file name and click the Save button:
The new master file is created and references to the original XML file
and all currently used slave files are inserted.
The new slave files are created and all routing states marked with a file
name are moved from the original XML file to the slave files.
All files are saved.
Note that the master file also can be entered as ROUTING_SETUP_FILE in the
SmartRDI: RDI_Configure file. This allows you to use any routing setup already
defined when debugging, even if you are editing only a single slave file.
Editing the slave files
Slave files contain outsourced routing states and also a copy of the global settings
and the control and configuration data of the original XML file and can therefore be
loaded independently from the other files to edit or add routing states.
Do not change the global settings and the control and configuration data when a
slave file is loaded. These changes will not be updated in the original XML file.
Note that in case the routing state selected in the "Failing-site Handling" table of the
Global Setup editor is not outsourced to the slave file, and error will be reported for
the global setup and the related entry will be highlighted in red. This behavior can
be ignored if the related routing state is not required for editing the slave file.
For debugging, we recommend always loading the master file with the file extension
".mfh" in order to gain access to all currently defined routing states.
Merging routing states
When loading a master file with the file extension ".mfh", the routing states of the
original XML file and of all used slave files are shown in the State setup editor.
Outsourced routing states can be recognized by the name of the slave file in the
"Master File Link" column.

__data__.text:
Outsourced routing states can be merged into the original XML file simply by
deleting the file name in the "Master File Link" column and saving the setup.
Some hints regarding merging routing states:
If a routing state with the same name is present multiple times in the original
XML file or in the slave files, the corresponding rows are highlighted in red in
the State Setup editor.
If a routing state is merged from a slave file into the original XML file, it is
deleted in the slave file unless it is the last state in that file. The slave file itself is
not deleted.
When merging slave files into the original XML file, slave files that are no longer
used are not automatically deleted. We therefore recommend cleaning up the
folders used if the slave files are no longer required. Finally, when slave files are no
longer required, the master file can also be deleted and the original XML file can be
used.
Importing routing states
Other files that have been created and modified outside of the Routing Tools editors
can be imported if no master file is used and the original target XML file is loaded.
To do this, however, the data of the other tabs must match. These are the global
settings and the control settings as well as the configuration settings.
A routing setup file can be imported into another routing setup file by right‑clicking
in the State Setup editor and selecting Import a state setup file.
Functional changes
Introduced in SmarTest 7.6.4
Routing Tools hardware
The Routing Tools support sequencer‑controlled utility lines and the PMUX01 Power
MUX card. These resources are controlled via serial interfaces that must be wired on the
DUT board.
Both Sequencer-controlled utility lines and the PMUX01 Power MUX can be controlled
by digital pins that are connected to the inputs of the serial interfaces.

Sequencer‑controlled utility lines
The utility lines feature a four-wire serial interface as shown below.
To make use of sequencer‑controlled utility lines you need to route four digital pins on
the DUT board to the appropriate serial interface pins. For more information, refer to
Sequencer-controlled utility lines.
For the pogo pin assignment of the utility pogo blocks refer to Pogo pin assignment -
Utility pogo blocks. The following signals are required for sequencer controlled utility
lines:
FRAMn: Frame, active low
SINP: Serial input to the FPGA on active wiring board
SCLK: Serial clock
SOUT: Optional serial output from the FPGA on active wiring board
The serial interface for sequencer‑controlled utility lines can handle the data stream for
more than one utility block. This cascading of serial interfaces of utility blocks is called
"ganging" in the context of the sequencer‑controlled utility lines. For more information,
refer to Sequencer-controlled utility lines - Ganging (cascading) pogo blocks.

Sequencer‑controlled utility lines
The serial interface of Sequencer-controlled utility lines is to be connected to four digital
pins. One set of four digital pins controls the serial interface of one single utility pogo
block or up to eight utility pogo blocks if ganging (cascading) of utility blocks is used.
Unlike shown in SmartRDI: Utility lines control, the control pins for the sequencer
controlled utility lines must be defined in the Routing Tools - Utility Lines Control editor
if the Routing Tools are to be used.
PMUX01 Power MUX
The IC interface of MUX cards is controlled by two digital pins. One pair of digital pins
can control a single MUX card or up to the maximum supported sixteen MUX cards.
The digital pins for controlling the IC interface of the MUX cards are to be defined by
the Routing Tools - PMUX Control editor.
Routing Tools setup file
The Routing Tools setup file holds all configuration data for software controlled utility
lines, sequencer‑controlled utility lines and the MUX cards. The predefined switch states
are also stored in this file. The file is created and stored by the Routing Tools editors.
The setup file to be loaded must be defined in the RDI_Configure file. For more
information, refer to keyword ROUTING_SETUP_FILE in topic SmartRDI: RDI_Configure
file.
Function rdi.route().downloadPmuxMemSet() must be called at least once in the test
program flow. The function does not only download the PMUX switch states but also
reads and processes the setup file.
Note  The function rdi.route().downloadPmuxMemSet() must be called at least once
in the test program flow even if only utility lines are controlled by the Routing Tools.

This class handles all routing states that have been defined by the Routing Tools editors.
The class translates the state setup table of the State Setup editor into executable
pattern and provides functions for downloading the MUX cards states to the setup
memory of the cards. The class additionally provides functions for applying or activating
the states, clearing all connections and modifying PMUX switches.
The created routeGroup object can only be accessed via the rdi() class.
Note  In SmartRDI, utility lines may be controlled by the rdi.util() class or by
the rdi.route() class of the Routing Tools. In addition, the utility lines may be
controlled by test method APIs, firmware commands or the "Routing Setup Tool".
This may lead to conflicts if the same utility line is controlled by more than one API
or tool.
For SmartRDI we therefore strongly recommend, controlling utility lines either by the
rdi.route() class or by the rdi.util() class. The mixed use of the two APIs or
other test method APIs and tools is not recommended. This recommendation
applies to code‑based programming and to pattern‑based programming.
Code‑based programming for the rdi.route() means that the utility lines are set
to "static" in the "Control table" of the Utility Lines Control editor. Pattern‑based
programming for the rdi.route() means that the utility lines are set to "dynamic"
in the "Utility Lines Control editor".

The function applies the selected routing state to the supported hardware. The selected
state may contain any combination of static utility lines, sequencer‑controlled utility
lines or PMUX switches. The applied routing state must already be defined by the State
Setup editor of the Routing Tools editors.
Only one routing state may be applied and activated at time.
Usage of the function:
The function can be called in the code‑based mode or in the pattern‑based mode.
For more information, refer to Execution mode in topic SmartRDI.
For debugging, we recommend setting the keyword ROUTING_ACK_CHECK of the
SmartRDI: RDI_Configure file to TRUE to enable a check if the routing state is
applied successfully to PMUX switches.
Execution sequence:
Code-based mode:
Combination of static utility lines and sequencer‑controlled utility lines or
PMUX switches:
The setup of the static utility lines is applied first, followed by a pattern that
applies the setup of the sequencer‑controlled utility lines and activates a stored
PMUX state.
Only sequencer‑controlled utility lines or PMUX switches:
A pattern that applies the setup of the sequencer‑controlled utility lines and
activates a stored PMUX state is started.
Pattern-based mode:
A pattern that applies the setup of the sequencer controlled utility lines and
activates a stored PMUX state is started within an RDI burst.
Note  Any routing state that contains static utility lines cannot be applied in
pattern‑based mode. This restriction ensures that the sequence of applying the
switch state corresponds to the source code.
Syntax

__data__.text:
The download routing states must already have been defined in the State Setup editor
of the Routing Tools editors.
Usage of the function:
The function is to be called in the code‑based mode. For more information, refer to
Execution mode in topic SmartRDI.
The function must be called at least once in the test program flow.
The first run can take several milliseconds due to time required for download.
This function automatically checks the Acknowledge bit of the IC bus to ensure
that the PMUX routing states successfully have been downloaded to the PMUX01
Power MUX cards. In case the download via the IC bus was not successful, the
function returns an error message:
Communication error, please check the connection to PMUX
To optimize the execution time, subsequent runs only check for changes. No new
download is performed if no changes are detected.
Important recommendations for optimizing the memory consumption:
The function should be called in a test suite with a tester frequency 2x the desired
PMUX speed (if PMUX is set to 1 MHz, the tester frequency needs to be 2 MHz).
The idea is to avoid having any type of padding or RPTV vectors either of which can
lead to excessive memory usage.
The function should be called in a separate port. Memory consumption is high if the
default port (@) is used as memory of non-PMUX control pins is also reserved.
Best practice: Create a port exclusively for PMUX (and utility line) control pins. This
recommendation applies only to this function. Ordinary rdi.route() class calls within
the program can but Do not necessarily have to use a separate port.
Note  The function does not only download the PMUX routing states but also reads
the setup file that has been defined in the SmartRDI: RDI_Configure file using
keyword ROUTING_SETUP_FILE. The function must therefore be called at least once
in the test program flow even if only utility lines are controlled by the Routing Tools.
The function re-reads the setup file only if the time-stamp has changed.
Note  The function can work with port() and the generated burst pattern is based
on the specified port. See Example 2.

__data__.text:
This class is a data container to define pins for direct access to the utility lines and PMUX
switches. The created ROUTE object can only be accessed via rdi.route().
The constructor of this class works similar to rdi.util().pin() and rdi.pmux().pin(). In
contrast to rdi.util() and rdi.pmux(), the rdi.route().pin() class expects a
switch name or a list of switch names that have been defined in the Utility Lines Config
editor or in the PMUX Config editor of the Routing Tools editors.
Usage of the function:
Depending on the target pin, the function can be called in the code‑based mode or
in the pattern‑based mode:
Software‑controlled (static) utility lines: Code‑based mode only
Sequencer‑controlled (dynamic) utility lines: Pattern‑based mode only
PMUX switches: Pattern‑based mode only
For more information, refer to Execution mode in topic SmartRDI.
The selected switches must already be defined in the Name column of the Utility
Lines Config editor or in the PMUX Config editor.
For debugging, we recommend setting the keyword ROUTING_ACK_CHECK of the
SmartRDI: RDI_Configure file to TRUE to enable a check if the route state is applied
successfully to PMUX switches.
Execution sequence:
Code-based mode:
Combination of static utility lines and sequencer‑controlled utility lines or
PMUX switches:
The new state of the static utility lines is applied first, followed by a pattern that
switches on or off the sequencer‑controlled utility lines and the selected PMUX
switches.
Only sequencer‑controlled utility lines or PMUX switches:
A pattern that switches on or off the sequencer‑controlled utility lines and the
selected PMUX switches is started.
Pattern-based mode:
A pattern that switches on or off the sequencer controlled utility lines and the
selected PMUX switches is started within an RDI burst.
Note  The switch settings for any pin definition that contains static utility lines
cannot be applied in pattern‑based mode. This restriction ensures that the
sequence of applying the switch settings corresponds to the source code.

rdi.route().showPmuxSensorStatus()
Reads the actual sensor values for temperature and humidity of all available MUX cards
and displays the values in the UI report window.
The functions displays additionally the thresholds for temperature and humidity alarms
and the alarm status. The alarm status is cleared when it is read and is therefore read
twice to get the latched status and the actual status:
Alarm History: The latched alarm status of the first read.
Alarm Actual: The current status of the alarm from the second read. The alarm
condition is still active if this value is not equal to 0x83.
Note  A PMUX01 card will automatically open all switches if the temperature
threshold or the humidity threshold is exceeded.
Usage of the function:
The function can be called only in the code‑based mode. For more information,
refer to Execution mode in topic SmartRDI.
The function displays suitable results only in online mode.
Calling this function requires about 500 milliseconds due to the internal sensor
cycle time.

The emap() class provides the following functions:
Overview of emap() class functions
Function Description Mode
Setup function:
rdi.emap().combinedFailCount() Return the total fail counts of multiple pins in one pattern label. P
rdi.emapLocation() Specify a location where error maps are stored.
rdi.emap().failCount() Return the number of failed cycles within a specified cycle range. P
rdi.emap().failCyc() Return all failed cycles' positions within a specified cycle range. P
rdi.emap().FFC() Return the number of the first failing cycle from a specified cycle range. P
rdi.emap().FFV() Specify a cycle number, starting from which the cycles in range are to be
checked for finding and retrieving the number of the first fail vector in
pattern.
P
rdi.emap().label() Specify a label to be executed. P
rdi.emap().multiFFC() Specify a start cycle and a number of failing cycles for retrieving a limited
number of failing cycles from a certain pattern cycle.
P
rdi.emap().pfMap() Return a pass/fail map for a specified cycle range. P
rdi.emap().startVec() Specify a start vector line in a user pattern. P
rdi.emap().stopVec() Insert STOP in user pattern. P
rdi.emap().xMode() Set the X-mode value for the pin that gets the error map result. P
Retrieval function:
rdi.id().getFailCount() Return the number of failed cycles for a specified pin.
rdi.id().getFailCyc() Return failing cycle positions.
rdi.id().getFFC() Return the number of the first failing cycle for a specified pin.
rdi.id().getPfMap() Return a pass/fail map for a specified pin.
rdi.id().getCombinedFailCount() Retrieve the total fail counts of many pins in just one label.
rdi.id().getFFV() Retrieve the number of the first fail vector in pattern for a specified pin.
rdi.id().getMultiFFC() Retrieve the number of failing cycles specified by multiFCC().

Parameter Description
startCyc The number of the first cycle in the cycle range in which the fails are counted. An integer. Cycle

The fail count and fail position are about "compare edge" (not tester cycle). So

The xMode parameter for a pin must be correct, otherwise the result for the pin
will not be correct.
The parameter specified in the function, such as startCyc and cycRange, is
about user cycles (edge), not tester cycles. This setting is critical when xMode is
set to be greater than 1.
For one pin, xMode must remain the same in different labels in burst; otherwise
the results might be wrong.

This function specifies a start vector line in a user pattern.

rdi.emap().stopVec()
Inserts STOP in a user pattern.
Both startVec() and stopVec() can be used to execute just part of a pattern, from a
startVec line to a stopVec line.
In the emap() class, startVec() and stopVec() can be used to create a pattern which
begins with the startVec() line and ends at the stopVec() line. From the new partial
pattern, the results of EMAP actions can be retrieved.
Restriction
There is a restriction on those specified vector lines who are near a sequencer
instruction in the test pattern. That is, the vector line specified in stopVec() should
never contain a sequencer instruction, and it should never immediately precede a vector
line which contains a sequencer instruction. See the figure below.
In the figure, rdi.func().startVec() and rdi.func().stopVec() are used to
illustrate the restriction. rdi.emap().startVec() and rdi.emap().stopVec() have
the same restriction.
This restriction is printed out in the Report window when the test is executed.

Note  For correctly retrieving the results of error map data:
For a specified pin, in one RDI_BEGIN/RDI_END block, its xMode number must
remain the same value, no matter it is for a SmartRDI command or in the user
pattern.
In the wavetable, the length of the device cycle name must align with the
xMode() value. For example, if you set xMode to xMode(2), the dvc must
correspondingly have two letters, such as "LL", "00", "11", "LL". Even the dvc of
the physical index f, which normal value is "." with SmartRDI, must be ".." for
xMode(2). Otherwise SmarTest cannot recognize the correct xMode value from
pattern.

SmartRDI: Functional test setup
SmartRDI provides the func() class to do functional tests.
The func() class provides a series of functions to identify a burst pattern, assign ID to a
pattern burst test, identify a label, specify a runtime label for each site, specify start and
stop lines in a user pattern, and other features. For more detailed information, see
SmartRDI class func().

rdi.burstId()
This function assigns ID to a pattern burst test. After the testing, this function stores the
pass/fail results of a pin, a group of pins, all pins or a port to buffer.
You must use this function before the setup of a burst pattern test. To read the result
from the buffer, use rdi.id().getBurstPassFail() at any time in your test method.
See id() and rdi.getBurstPassFail() for more information.
You must place this function inside an RDI_BEGIN()/RDI_END() block, otherwise
rdi.id().getBurstPassFail() always returns a PASS result.
Note  If the SmartRDI alarm handling is used, the burst pass/fail result is impacted
by an alarm fail. This means if an alarm check fails, the burst result will fail too.

rdi.func().stopVec()
Inserts STOP in user pattern.
In the emap() class, startVec() and stopVec() can be used to create a pattern which
begins with the startVec() line and ends at the stopVec() line. From the new partial
pattern, the results of EMAP actions can be retrieved.
Restriction
There is a restriction on those specified vector lines who are near a sequencer
instruction in the test pattern. That is, the vector line specified in stopVec() should
never contain a sequencer instruction, and it should never immediately precede a vector
line which contains a sequencer instruction. See the figure below.
This restriction is printed out in the Report window when the test is executed.

SmartRDI: General topics and functions
SmartRDI provides some general functions for setting up multiple types of tests.
The working scope of general SmartRDI commands is test suite. This means that a
general command resumes its original setup after the test suite has been executed. For
example rdi.setPinStatus("A",1), this command specifies the default status of pin A in the
current test suite to 1. The value 1 will not be valid after the test suite has been
executed. If you need the status of pin A to be 1 again, you must set the command
again in the next test suite.

About this task
Runtime values can be defined and applied as
common value that is applied to all active sites or as
array of site-specific values.
This task covers both the common runtime value and site-specific runtime values. Both
solutions support the code‑based mode and pattern‑based mode.
For setting site-specific PPMU voltage levels as runtime values, SmartRDI features a fast
transfer mode that shortens the test time in high-site-count applications. For more
information, refer to PPMU fast transfer mode of SmartRDI.

Procedure
1. Define a variable that holds the runtime value(s):
Common value: Create a variable for a runtime value that applies to all active
sites.
Site-specific values: Create an array for the site-specific runtime values.
Resize the array so that it matches to the number of all configured sites.
Initialize the entire array to a reasonable value.
Supported types of runtime values are defined in the syntax section of
rdi.runTimeVal().
2. Set the runtime value(s):
Common value: Set the created variable to the value that should be applied to
all active sites.
Site-specific values: Within a FOR_EACH_SITE loop, fill the created array for all
active sites with the site-specific values.
3. Pass the created individual value or array to function rdi.runTimeVal() using a
unique name string as identifier.
4. Use the unique name string as input parameter for a function that supports runtime
values.

Basic rules to consider
With fast transfer mode enabled, SmartRDI will automatically use the mode if the
following rules are met. Otherwise, the normal transfer mode is used:
The fast transfer mode can be used only with Smart Scale test head cards.
The fast transfer mode is only supported for site-specific PPMU voltage levels that

Common runtime values and other PPMU settings are not supported.
The fast transfer mode is not supported for resources shared between active sites.
The following error message is issued if shared resources are used:
ERROR: MTRA - mismatch between number of sites selected and number 
Using the fast transfer mode
The fast transfer mode is to be enabled for the entire testflow using keyword
FAST_PPMU_LEVEL_TRANSFER in the SmartRDI: RDI_Configure file.
The fast transfer mode requires that a minimum fast transfer buffer size of 131072 bytes
is specified in the Technology file for a device. Otherwise the following error message is
issued:
ERROR: MTRA - ... a minimum fast transfer buffer size of 131072 bytes

Controlling burst site upload
SmartRDI supports "burst site upload" capacity for DC and digital capture results.
The data upload time for high site counts but low data sizes is mainly influenced by the
FW query per site. The "burst site upload" capacity uploads all results over all sites by
one FW query to achieve a better throughput.
SmarTest 7.4.2.1 provides a new capability to perform "burst site upload" for digital
capture results. SmartRDI 2.4.5.1 supports this capability with options to enable and
disable it:
The keyword DIGCAP_BURST_SITE_UPLOAD in SmartRDI: RDI_Configure file
provides a global control of enabling and disabling "burst site upload" for digital
capture results.
The test method rdi.digCapBurstSiteUpload() provides a local control which
overwrites the global control setting.
SmarTest 7.4.3 supports the upload of DC results over sites in one burst. SmartRDI 2.5.0
supports this capability with an option to enable and disable it:
The keyword DC_BURST_SITE_UPLOAD in SmartRDI: RDI_Configure file provides a
global control of enabling and disabling "burst site upload" for DC results.

RDI_BEGIN()
RDI_BEGIN() and RDI_END() define and enclose an RDI block. The RDI block marks a
section in a test method to set up and execute tests in the pattern‑based mode of
SmartRDI.
RDI_BEGIN() and RDI_END() are intended to be used in the ON_FIRST_INVOCATION
block and must always be implemented together.
For the first run, SmartRDI creates corresponding pattern from the code within the RDI
block. Depending on the value of parameter mode, the single patterns or a pattern burst
that contains all generated patterns for the RDI block are executed for the first and all
subsequent runs.
The code inside RDI_BEGIN()/RDI_END() is only executed in the first run after
build. This is required for generating pattern content.
In the following runs, the code inside RDI_BEGIN()/RDI_END() is skipped! This is
because the pattern content is already available.
DO NOT put any code that you would like to run in EACH execution into
RDI_BEGIN()/RDI_END().
For debugging a project: At the line where RDI_END() is located, the pattern which
has been created in the first run is executed.
XXX(data type) result = rdi.id().getXxxx();
const ARRAY_D &Result = rdi.id("cap").getWaveform("DATA_1");
ARRAY_D results = rdi.id("meas").getMultiValue("pinA");
rdi.id("id").getAlarmPassFail("A");

TA::BURST: Pattern-based execution mode. This is the default mode.
TA::SINGLE: Single step execution mode for debugging.

Execution modes in RDI_BEGIN()
Burst Mode (TA::BURST)
This is the target mode for developing tests. This mode is the default mode if
parameter mode is not specified.
First run after build:
One or more patterns are generated for all RDI commands of the RDI
block.Note:
RDI commands are enclosed by rdi.class() and rdi.execute().
A pattern burst, containing all generated patterns for the RDI block, is
generated.
First run after build and all subsequent runs:
The pattern burst runs at the end of the RDI block when RDI_END() is
executed.
Single Mode (TA::SINGLE)
This mode should be used only for debugging.
The Single Mode works similar to the Burst Mode but utilizes more pattern bursts:
In Burst Mode, one pattern burst is executed per RDI block.
In Single Mode, one pattern burst is executed per RDI command that is
enclosed by rdi.class() and rdi.execute().
The Single Mode allows you therefore, using the debugger to execute the RDI
commands within an RDI block step by step.
Production Mode (TA::PROD)
The non-generation mode for production.
Works similarly as TA::BURST, but WITHOUT setup generation.
SmartRDI just follows the naming rules to run the needed setups.
User still needs to keep alignment between the code and the setup. Result
retrieval information is still based on the code.
SmartRDI does not create any pattern or setup in Production Mode. You must
therefore ensure, that the following requirements are met:
Pattern in RDI block:
A pattern setup file must be available.

Required pattern of the RDI blocks are to be generated by SmartRDI with
parameter mode of the RDI blocks set to TA::BURST.
The pattern setup file must be saved after it has been modified by
SmartRDI: The modified file is marked by an asterisk "*" in the Test Program
Explorer.
The pattern setup file must be added to the Setups page of the Flow Data
Editor.
Analog setups:
Setups for analog cards (AWG and DGT) are automatically generated by
SmartRDI. Minimum an analog control file must be available. AWG setups also
require an analog waveform file.
1. Add both the analog control file and (for AWG tests) the analog waveform
file in the Setups page of the Flow Data Editor.
2. Ensure that parameter SETUP_UPTODATE in file SmartRDI: RDI_Configure
file is set to FALSE.
3. Reload all setups.
4. Ensure that all required files are loaded: Analog control file and (for AWG
tests) the analog waveform file.
5. Start the full flow with parameter mode of the RDI blocks set to TA::BURST
to allow SmartRDI generating the setup and the waveform.
6. Verify that both the analog control file and (for AWG tests) the analog
waveform file are marked by an asterisk "*".
7. Save both the analog control file and (for AWG tests) the analog waveform
file.

filled with waveform data, but accessed in sequencer program ...

rdi.portSync()
Creates a dummy pattern to synchronize the pattern of different ports in a multiport
test.
It can be used to synchronize the patterns of all ports or synchronize the patterns of
selected ports.
Note  During the calculation of synchronization cycles, a trade-off is made between
synchronization accuracy and additional test time (by adding synchronization
cycles). If port periods are an integer multiple of each other, you may achieve 100%
synchronization. For best results, ensure to have a least common integer multiple of
the periods of all ports.

synchronization.
The CTIM instructions change test setup to the current timing set and achieve port synchronization.

Generating an ORE template file for each execution
In SmartRDI 7.6.1, you can add the test results of each execution into an ORE template
file. SmartRDI provides a function rdi.startNextOreTemp() to define a separate point
between executions so the template file generation for each execution can be achieved.
The ORE result after the separate point will be put into a new template file named
rdi_ore_template_by_user_code_N.xml. Here, N stands for a number starting from
0. In the first run, rdi_ore_template_by_user_code_0.xml will be generated for the
first execution; in the second run, rdi_ore_template_by_user_code_1.xml will be
generated for the second execution.
See also rdi.startNextOreTemp().

ARRAY results in the template file
For ARRAY value type, the result size may be very big. It is not possible to check all the
results in the template file.
If the result size is less than 200, SmartRDI inserts all the results to the XML file.
If the result size is equal to or greater than 200, SmartRDI inserts all the results into
a .txt file which is located in the same folder as the
rdi_ore_template_by_user_code.xml. SmartRDI also adds the path information
in the .xml file.

Elements in an ORE file
Elements Description
<offlineResultEmulation> Root element of the ORE file.
<testSuite> The test suite that contains the result retrieval command.
Optional.
Skipping this element means "any" test suite.
<id> The SmartRDI result ID.
Mandatory.
It supports string and integer IDs.
string id example: <id name = "id1">
integer id example: <id name = "__1__">
<pin> The measuring pin.
Mandatory in most cases.
Comma separated pin lists are supported; pin groups must be expanded to pin
lists.
For special cases like per-label Pass/Fail results, <pin> is inapplicable.
<site> Supports different results on different sites.
Optional.
Skipping this element means all sites are selected.

The <alarm> element
This element stores the results of alarm checking performed through the SmartRDI's
alarm() class.
Retrieving the ORE result of alarm handling
The <alarm> element stores alarm checking results in its passFail attribute. The
attribute saves the pass/fail information which will be retrieved by the getAlarmPassFail()
function.
Get Result Function in SmartRDI ORE File Syntax Example
int getAlarmPassFail (); <alarm passFail = "1"/>
See the Example 1.
Generating an ORE template for alarm handling
For the alarm class, if ORE_TEMPLATE_BY_USER_CODE = TRUE is set in the SmartRDI:
RDI_Configure file, SmartRDI will add alarming handling results to the
rdi_ore_template_by_user_code.xml path.
Note  SmartRDI can only add the alarm handling result which has been specified by
the rdi.id("id").getAlarmPassFail("*"); in the test method.
See the Example 2.

The <cogo> element
This element stores results of COGO judgment performed using the SmartRDI's cogo()
class.
The <cogo> element stores COGO judgment results in its searchResult,
searchRiseResult, searchFallResult and searchPath attributes. The
searchResult attribute saves COGO judgment results returned by a
getSearchResult() function; the searchRiseResult attribute saves COGO judgment
results returned by a getSearchRiseResult() function; the searchFallResult
attribute saves COGO judgment results returned by a getSearchFallResult()
function; the searchPath attribute saves COGO judgment results returned by a
getSearchPath() function.
Get Result Function in SmartRDI ORE File Syntax Example
double getSearchResult(); <cogo searchResult="2.15" />
double getSearchRiseResult(); <cogo searchRiseResult="3.15" />
double getSearchFallResult(); <cogo searchFallResult="4.15" />
ARRAY_I getSearchPath(); <cogo searchPath = "0,0,1,1,0,1" />
Example
Below is an example of the <cogo> element and its corresponding SmartRDI code block.
An ORE file containing <cogo> elements:
The corresponding SmartRDI code block that can generate this ORE file:
<id name = "cogo1">
  <cogo searchResult= "3.15" />
  <cogo searchPath= "0,0,0,1" /> 
</id>
RDI_BEGIN();
  rdi.cogo("cogo1").search(TA::LINEAR)
     .pathPin("DATA3").start(0).stop(3)
     .step(6).blockBegin();
...
  rdi.cogo().search().blockEnd();
RDI_END();
...
rdi.id("cogo1").getSearchResult(); // {3.15}
rdi.id("cogo1").getSearchPath();   // {0,0,0,1}

The <dc> element
This element stores the results of a DC test performed by the SmartRDI's dc() class.
Topic 343531

The <dc> element stores value test results in its value and burstValue attributes, and
waveform test results in its waveform, currentWaveform and voltageWaveform
attributes.
The value attribute saves DC value test results returned by a getValue() or
getMultiValue() function, while burstValue attribute saves results returned by
getBurstValue().
The waveform attribute saves DC waveform test results returned by a getWaveform()
function; the voltageWaveform attribute saves DC waveform test results returned by a
getVoltageWaveform() function; the currentWaveform attribute saves DC waveform
test results returned by a getCurrentWaveform() function.
Get Result Function in SmartRDI ORE File Syntax Example
double getValue(pin); <dc value = "1.23" />
ARRAY_D& getMultiValue(pin); Multiple entries of <dc value = "1.23"/>
or
<dc multiValue = "-1.22,1.23"/>
<dc multiValue = "./ORE/waveform"/>
ARRAY_D& getBurstValue(pin); <dc burstValue = "-1.22,1.23" />
or
<dc burstValue = "./ORE/waveform" />
ARRAY_D& getWaveform(pin); <dc waveform = "-1.22,1.23" />
or
<dc waveform = "./ORE/waveform" />
ARRAY_D& getVoltageWaveform(pin); <dc voltageWaveform = "-1.22,1.23" />
or
<dc voltageWaveform = "./ORE/waveform" />
ARRAY_D& getCurrentWaveform(pin); <dc currentWaveform = "-1.22,1.23" />
or
<dc currentWaveform = "./ORE/waveform" />

Pass/Fail per label with digital capture
SmartRDI automatically changes to the ERMP mode when both digital capture and per-
label pass/fail exist in the same RDI_BEGIN/RDI_END block.
The reason is that the FW command FLBL cannot work together with
DIGITAL_CAPTRUE_TEST().
In addition, ERMP cannot work with a pin for digital capture. Therefore, if you use the
per-label Pass/Fail feature to retrieve pass/fail results on a digital capture pin, you
cannot get the right pass/fail results. A warning will pop up when this happens.
Also, the keyword PER_LABEL_FUNC_RESULT_NO_BREAK_VEC must be set to TRUE, see
SmartRDI: RDI_Configure file.
The Pass/Fail label must contain 8 or more vectors to work with digital capture.

RDI_BEGIN();
  rdi.smartVec().pin("Pin1")
                .writeData(20,8,2)
                .pin("Pin2")
                .expectData(20,2)
                .execute();
  rdi.func().label("Label1")
            .execute();
RDI_END();

Pure generation mode
When pure generation mode is enabled, SmartRDI only generates setups for pattern,
burst, DC event, analog set, and others. At the same time SmartRDI skips pattern
execution and result upload.
As a result, all rdi...getXxxx() calls such as getVector(), getReadBit(),
getWaveform() return dummy results. The size of result arrays = 0.
This pure generation mode is supported through the keyword
PURE_GENERATION_MODE in SmartRDI: RDI_Configure file or rdi.pureGenerationMode()
in SmartRDI code.
PURE_GENERATION_MODE works globally for SmartRDI actions while
rdi.pureGenerationMode() targets a test suite locally at one time.
When this feature is enabled, Viasco bind is omitted by the execution in the first run,
which can shorten the total first run time. The generated setups for pattern, burst, DC
event, analog set, and others can be saved for reuse later or in other test programs.

true in your SmartRDI: RDI_Configure file as follows:

Register structure
Register structure is based on a CMSIS-SVD XML hierarchy. A CMSIS-SVD XML file
normally contains the structure description of a single device. The file must be
converted to a C++ structure before the register structure can be used in test methods.
Topic 351643

Here is a typical CMSIS-SVD XML Hierarchy:
According to CMSIS-SVD , an SVD file usually describes the structure of a device. A
device is formed of a processor and at least one peripheral. Each peripheral has at least
one register. A register can have one or more fields. The range of values for a field can
be further described with enumerated values.
Peripheral level, register level, and field level are the main levels handled in register
operations. They are described by CMSIS-SVD as follows.
Peripheral level
A peripheral is a named collection of registers. A peripheral is mapped to a defined
base address within the device's address space. A peripheral allocates one or more
exclusive address blocks relative to its base address, such that all described registers
fit into the allocated address blocks. Allocated addresses without an associated
register description are automatically considered reserved. The peripheral can be
assigned to a group of peripherals and may be associated with one or more
interrupts.
Register level
A register is a named, programmable resource that belongs to a peripheral. Registers
are mapped to a defined address in the address space of the device. An address is
specified relative to the peripheral base address. The description of a register
documents the purpose and function of the resource. A debugger requires
information about the permitted access to a resource as well as side effects
triggered by read and write accesses respectively.
Field level

Registers may be partitioned into chunks of bits of distinct functionality. A chunk is
referred to as field. The field names within a single register must be unique. Only
architecturally defined fields shall be described. Any bits not being explicitly
described are treated as reserved. They are not displayed in the System Viewer and
are padded in the bit fields of the device header file. The case-insensitive field
named "reserved" is treated as a keyword and each field with this name is ignored.
For more detailed information about the CMSIS-SVD XML Hierarchy, refer to SVD
Description (*.svd) Format on the CMSIS-SVD website.

Note  This task is optional. You can do most of register access setups without a
register structure. But without register structure definitions, you cannot perform
RMW (Read-Modify-Write) operations.

The register access library has been implemented.

Procedure
1. Create a folder in the working directory, for example gen.
2. Use the provided script RegisterAccessRegisterGen to convert your device's
SVD file (*.svd) to a C++ register structure, for example:
/opt/hp93000/soc64_7.6.0_*_*/prod_com/rdi/lbin/RegisterAccessRegist
-i <svd file path> -o ./gen -N Example
If the conversion is successful, the following message shows: RegisterAccess Gen
is successfully finished!.
The converted register structure files will show in the gen folder, including the
peripherals folder, registers folder, Example_AllDevices.cpp, and
Example_AllDevices.h.
For example,
The RegisterAccessRegisterGen script is located in
/opt/hp93000/soc*.*/prod_com/rdi/lbin/.

/opt/hp93000/soc/prod_com/rdi/lbin/RegisterAccessRegisterGen --
help
to show the definition of -i, -o, -N, -a, and -s.
3. Copy the converted source files to your test method source folder.

Protocol management
A protocol used for the RA library is a set of rules for how to do data transactions
between devices and a tester. A protocol only defines a unique class.
The RA library natively supports protocol classes for I2C, JTAG, and SPI. The three
protocol class templates are available. You can customize a template or create a
protocol class based on the template and predefined transactions.
Available templates:

JTAG protocol class template
SPI protocol class template
Predefined transactions:

JTAG predefined transactions
SPI predefined transactions
To use a protocol class, you must put the protocol .cpp file somewhere in your test
method project. For example, /workspaces/david/TM/src/protocols/MyI2C.cpp, in
which MyI2C.cpp is the protocol class file.

virtual void defineWriteRegister(I2C& i2c, ULONG64 address, ULONG64 dat

Usage of register operations in test method
Register operations can be performed in test methods through the RA library. The
register operation commands must be put in an RDI_BEGIN/RDI_END block.
Register operations can be done even when no register structure definitions exist. But
without the help of register structure definitions, RMW operations cannot be performed.
The RA library supports the structure of a register to be represented in the code. For
example, PERIPHERAL0 stands for a peripheral, REGISTER0 stands for a register under
the peripheral. Therefore the WRITE command for the REGISTER0 in test methods can
be reg.PERIPHERAL0().REGISTER0().setValue(0x55).write();.
In the WRITE command example above, reg is a user-defined macro and must be
already defined at the beginning of your test methods, for example,
#define reg RA::<className in your xxx_AllDevices.h>::getInstance().
You can name the macro any name that is suitable.

Learning mode
In the learning mode, the following actions will be done in sequence internally in the RA
library for RMW operations :
1. Read original values from all the registers on which RMW operations are to be
performed.
2. Save the values to Register Cache.
3. Overwrite bit fields to be modified.
4. Write all the registers.
The read operations, which are performed on all related RMW registers, read bit field
values and save the values to a file as Register Cache (RC).
All the changes of register values are tracked in sequence according to write operations
on registers.
In the learning mode, two burst patterns are generated for each RDI_BEGIN/RDI_END
block.
Normal pattern, which contains all the actions defined in the block.
Auxiliary burst pattern, which is generated by the RA library to read values from
RMW-related registers before write operations are performed.
Each burst that has RMW operations must have a corresponding auxiliary burst
generated.

Production mode
The production mode does not have the reading step.
This mode has a Check action:
1. Check: read values from all registers and compare the values to those saved in RC.
This action is optional and can be skipped.
By default, this action is disabled. Use
RA_CFG.setDefaultCheckMode(RA::CHK_VAL) or
RA_SET_CHECK_MODE(RA::CHK_VAL) to enable this action.
2. Use specified bit field values to replace the corresponding part in the whole register
value which is stored in RC.
In the Check operation, the tester reads the values of RMW registers and compares
them to the corresponding values saved in RC.
In this mode, a normal burst pattern is generated for each RDI_BEGIN/RDI_END block.
The main patterns for Check are generated and put at the beginning of the burst
pattern of an RDI_BEGIN/RDI_END block.
The mode is set by RA_CFG.setDefaultMode(RA_MODE mode) in test suite or
RA_SET_MODE(RA::MODE) before an RDI_BEGIN/RDI_END block. See Example 2.
Register Cache
Register Cache is only required by RMW operations.
RC is represented by a file for each burst. The RC file is automatically generated in the
learning mode and it has an .rcf extension. The values of RMW registers are saved to
the file and these values can be read back by operations in the production mode. If the
Check action is enabled in the production mode, RC files are used to compare with the
actual registers values read back from DUT.
The RC files must exist in the production mode. Otherwise an error message is
displayed.
Be default, RC files are located in the test program folder. You can use
RA_CFG.setRegisterCacheFilePath("./rcf"); to specify a location for your RC
files.

For concepts and detailed information refer to SmartCalc framework.
For a list of all SMC related test method APIs, refer to SMC_... (SmartCalc API reference).
Basic structure
A test suite, based on SmartRDI, utilizes the same structure as a test method that uses
test method APIs only:
Background processes are armed by the SMC_ARM() function or the variants of this
function. Each SMC_ARM() call creates a new thread. For more information, refer to
SMC_... (SmartCalc API reference).
The background process itself is defined as public SMC_backgroundProcessing()
function within the test method class of the test suite.
The SmartRDI functions used for the setup and used to retrieve the data are the
same for tests utilizing hidden upload and tests without hidden upload: Just the
functions to retrieve the results are to be moved from the run() function to the
SMC_backgroundProcessing() function.
SmartRDI uses rdi.hiddenUpload() to enable the hidden upload feature, which
allows SmartRDI to perform the upload of data in the SMC_backgroundProcessing()
function of the test suite.
Ensure that SMC gets enough time to access the hardware in the background
threads. For more information, refer to Hide analog and digital data upload in
SmartCalc recommendations.
For general information on how to implement an SMC test, refer to Four-step SmartCalc
implementation in the SmartCalc framework documentation.

Thread per site and common thread
Each function call and each thread takes some time overhead for preparation and
cleanup. This overhead in test time depends also on the ratio of function calls and
threads and the number of available CPU cores. For high-site-count applications, the
overhead might exceed the benefit of using background threads or hidden uploads
respectively.
The SmartCalc framework supports therefore two implementations of background
processes:
Thread per site
The "Thread per site" is armed by SMC_ARM() or the variants of this function outside
of the ON_FIRST_INVOCATION block. The "Thread per site" is recommended for low
site-count applications.
Common thread
The "Common thread" (also know as "Single thread") is armed by SMC_ARM() or the
variants of this function inside of the ON_FIRST_INVOCATION block. The "Common
thread" is recommended for high site-count applications.
For more information, refer to SmartCalc "Thread per site" and "Common thread".
CAUTION Within a test suite, SmartRDI supports either the implementation
"Thread per site" or "Common thread" with one thread for all active sites.
Mixing the two solutions by assigning multiple active sites to more than one thread
(multisite per thread) is not supported and can lead to invalid logging of results. For
example: A solution with 16 sites and 4 threads is not supported.

About this task
SmartRDI provides the rdi.hiddenUpload() function to enable the hidden upload
functionality. The functions to retrieve the test result with the hidden upload are the
same functions to retrieve the test result without hidden upload.
Procedure
1. In the run() function of the test method class,
a. Enable the hidden upload with the function rdi.hiddenUpload().
b. Execute the test as usual in an RDI block.
c. Start the hidden upload with SMC_ARM().
2. Retrieve the result with SmartRDI get...() functions in the public method
SMC_backgroundProcessing() of the test method class. No unique result ID is
required for the result retrieval functions.

Note  In the first run after build/TM termination, SmartRDI will do normal uploads
instead of hidden uploads for all user-specified hidden-upload results. The purpose
is to prevent the conflict between hidden uploads and setup generation.

SmartRDI: Level and timing set changes
SmartRDI provides level() and timing() classes with a set() function to change
the level set and timing set.
In the pattern‑based mode, the rdi.timing().set() command will create a
dummy pattern with CTIM and the rdi.level().set() command will create a
dummy pattern with CLEV. See the code example in Example 1.
In the code‑based mode, the rdi.timing().set() command or the
rdi.level().set() command will change the primary timing set or level set.
In pattern‑based mode, the timing or level set will be reset to the primary set after
the pattern-burst ends with RDI_END(). This is a standard SmarTest behavior, not an
RDI feature.
In code‑based mode, the timing or level set remains unchanged until a new primary
set is specified.
Note  If you are dealing with multiport:
The number of level or timing change actions on different ports must be the
same.
If BFLM mode is used for not generating break vectors between patterns, the
generated dummy pattern will contain padding vectors that may get the ports
out of synchronization. You must add a rdi.portSync() command in the
subsequent code line to synchronize the ports again.

SmartRDI: Pattern-based conditional jump
- cogo
SmartRDI provides the cogo() class and related functions for pattern judgment and
searching.
Topic 149524

Cogo introduction
The cogo() class has the name from "conditional go". This class provides the functions
for specifying and executing conditional jump into different labels to judge
pattern‑based on pass/fail. The cogo() class can also execute a binary or linear search
based on pattern. The following diagram gives an overview of the operation of the
cogo() class.
The cogo() class has the following functions:

Judgment in cogo
The following code snippet is an example of how the cogo() class to judge a pattern
pass or fail.
The example above utilizes optional pairs of curly brackets "{" and "}" for the
RDI_BEGIN()/RDI_END() block and for the block that is enclosed by
rdi.cogo()...begin() and rdi.cogo()...end(). These optional curly brackets
enclose the complete code within the blocks and are used for simplifying the correct
indentation with assistance of the related Eclipse tool.
The judgment command inside rdi.cogo().node().begin()/end() must be a
command with a pass or fail result.
Some suitable commands that return pass or fail include:
rdi.func().label("abc").execute();
rdi.smartVec()...expectData()/expectBit().execute();
rdi.dc()...limit(low,high).execute(); for PPMU and DC Scales pins. Refer
to DC Scale hardware support for cogo pass/fail judgment for more information.
Note  In cogo judgment, all of limit(low,high),
limit(TA::NO_LIMIT,high) and limit(low,TA::NO_LIMIT) support AVI64
cards. But limit(low,high) does not work with other DC Scale cards while
both limit(TA::NO_LIMIT,high) and limit(low,TA::NO_LIMIT) support
other DC Scale cards.
Note  valueMode(TA::SA) is used for cogo judgment. valueMode(TA::BADC) is
used for measuring results inside cogo blocks but cannot be used for judgment.
Note  When dc() and limit() work together in a cogo block, they can only
provide pass/fail results and cannot provide value results.
Note  For digital dc, limit() must work together with iForce()/vForce();
otherwise limits will not be applied for cogo judgment.
The pass/fail result of the pattern before a cogo block may have an impact on the
pass/fail result of the first cogo judgment.

pass/fail result of the first cogo judgment is to be fail too even if the result of the first
cogo is actually pass.
Note  Do not use commands with pass/fail results right before a cogo block. The
results may affect the first cogo judgment.

System-reserved waiting in cogo
The system needs a waiting time to make the judgment. This waiting time lies between
the judgment pattern and the jump at the end of the cogo execution. This waiting time
is not a fixed value and it depends on its environment.
You can put your own rdi.wait() function before cogo().node().end(). If you use
rdi.cogo().wait(double) in your code, SmartRDI can check whether this waiting
time is long enough for the system-reserved waiting.
Example:
Note  If there are any shared pin cross sites, you must set the test suite flag
"site_match" to ON.

Important rules
Below are some important rules you need to follow, in order to achieve a successful
usage of the COGO feature:
1. If there is a DC value measurement inside a "free cogo branching" or "linear
search", the result and ID mapping will not work after the COGO block because the
number of measurements is unpredictable, but the user is still able to use
getBurstValue(pin) to retrieve all DC measurement results of this pin.
2. The awg(), dgt(), rfs(), rfm() and digCap() classes cannot be put into a
cogo()...begin()/cogo()...end() block, nor a cogo()...blockBegin()/
cogo()...blockEnd() block.
3. Because neither COGO execution time nor cycle number is predictable, a
portSync() function that follows a cogo() command within one RDI_BEGIN()/
RDI_END() block may not work.
4. Use rdi.cogo().wait(double) for the judgment latency.
5. In a COGO block, NO additional DCS (DPS/SIG) measurements are allowed on the
same port, or on different ports with the same sequencing group. Otherwise it
would corrupt the pass/fail judgment. However, additional PPMU/BADC
measurements are supported inside a COGO block.
6. COGO supports only one port in the COGO structure.
7. Only one Binary Search COGO structure is supported within one RDI_BEGIN()/
RDI_END() block. For other COGO structures there is no such limitation.
8. You must set the global and the local (test suite) Site Match flags to ON.
9. If the Fast Sync is used (ON), you need to set the Site Match flag to OFF.
10. For Linear Search
the .start() input -> FAIL judgment
the .stop() input -> PASS judgment
11. For Binary Search
the .start() input -> PASS judgment
the .stop() input -> FAIL judgment
12. rdi.cogo().pathPin() must not receive any signal from the DUT board.
13.

13. If rdi.cogo().pathPin() is not used, an RDI_BEGIN/RDI_END block can have one cogo
search block only.
14. A DUT board calibration might be required to ensure correct functionality of the
path pin at higher pattern speeds, for example, a cycle time greater than 50 MHz.

15. Except for the dc result retrieved by getBurstValue(), all types of measurements
inside a cogo block cannot provide ID-based values due to the cogo's execution
number is not predictable.

rdi.cogo().wait()
Specifies a system wait time that occurs after pass or fail judgment. Within this time,
SmartRDI waits for the pass/fail judgment to be propagated.
If you do not specify a value for this function, SmartRDI uses the EPRC? firmware
command to automatically calculate an appropriate time period for waiting.

period is long enough. If the period is not long enough, the report window displays an
event message, for example, cogo().wait(0.001) is not enough at port A to
make cogo judgment. It needs 0.2 us at least for this cogo node.

Accessing PMUX sensors
The PMUX card has sensors for detecting temperature and relative humidity. SmartRDI
provides APIs to get access to these sensors. PMUX switches can open automatically if
the threshold specified by a setting API is exceeded.
Topic 152284

SmartRDI provides the following functions to access PMUX sensors:
To set temperature and humidity's alarm thresholds:
setTempThresh()
setHumThresh()
To read temperature and humidity's alarm thresholds from the hardware into the
software cache:
readTempThresh()
readHumThresh()
To read the measured temperature and humidity from the sensor into the software
cache:
readTempSensor()
readHumSensor()
readAlarm()
To retrieve the results from the software cache:
getTempThresh()
getHumThresh()
getTempSensor()
getHumSensor()
getAlarm()

For SmarTest version 7.4.4 and higher, we recommend using the more comfortable

Do not mix programming by the Routing tools and the rdi.route() class with the

programming in one program.
Pin definitions
The control pins are to be defined as digital pins in the Pin setting editors. Two pins
must be defined per IC bus:
The SDA pin controls the serial data line of the bus. This pin must be defined as IO
pin.
The SCL pin generates the clock on the serial clock line of the bus. This pin is a drive
only pin that is never used for reading. The pin can therefore be defined as I pin or
as IO pin.
2

Pin configuration
The used digital pins must be defined in the SmartRDI: RDI_Configure file. The keyword
PMUX_X_CTRL followed by two digital pins defines the IC interface of each MUX card:
All used MUX cards must be defined in the RDI configure file.
The "X" in the PMUX_X_CTRL keyword is to be replaced with the number 1 … 16 of
the MUX card. Refer to MUX cards filling rules for more information regarding the
numbering of the MUX card and PMUX01 addressing scheme for the correct
addressing of the MUX cards.
Two pins are to be inserted after the PMUX_X_CTRL keyword: The first pin defines
the SDA pin. The second pin defines the SCL pin.
The SDA pin and the SCL pin must be assigned to different digital channels.
The definitions for the SDA pin and the SCL pin may be re-used for other cards.
Other pins may be used for SDA and SCL in case more than one IC bus per site
should be defined.
For a detailed description of the MUX related parameters in the RDI_Configure file, refer
to table PMUX setup in SmartRDI: RDI_Configure file.
For more information regarding the assignment to sites and multi-site handling refer to
PMUX01 programming overview.
The example below shows how to define six MUX cards 1 ... 3 and 5 ... 7 that are
assigned to two IC buses per site. MUX cards 1 and 5 are assigned to the first IC bus
that is controlled by pins SDA_1 and SCL_1. The other cards are assigned to the second
I C bus that is controlled by pins SDA_2 and SCL_2:

For information regarding the recommended values refer to PMUX01 control pins.

Timing
The timing of the generated pattern must comply with the standard IC timing. The
following timing definitions are required for the digital pins that control the IC bus:
The period in the example above is derived from the spec variable cycleTime that is
also used to define the position of the edges. The timing can be defined separately for
the SDA pins and the SCL pins and can be defined in on block if both the SDA pins and
the SCL pins are defined as IO pins.
CAUTION Drive edge 1 for SCL must be set to a negative value to comply with
the required IC timing. The value must be -50 % of the cycle time.
Example
The pattern, generated by SmartRDI can be inspected in the pattern editor. The
following diagram shows an example for the generated pattern.
MUX cards I2C timing
The diagram above shows that the SCL signal is shifted to the left by half of the cycle
time to fit to the IC protocol. The read data strobe is placed at 50 % of the cycle: Data
are valid a short time after the falling edge of SCL in the previous cycle. SmartRDI uses
minimum two pattern cycles per SCL clock cycle to fulfill the requirements of the IC
protocol. Padding vectors are inserted automatically for pattern rates that exceed the
maximum frequency of the IC bus.

SmartRDI: RDI_Configure file
The RDI_Configure file is used to configure some default settings to be used when
programming with SmartRDI. The RDI_Configure file is in folder testmethod of the
loaded device. An RDI_Configure.Template file will be generated in the first run,
which has all options with comments.
These settings include setting the default pin status, configuring the RF trigger pin,
configuring the trigger pin for MSDPS/GPDPS pin, configuring the sequencer‑controlled
utility lines, specifying the default RF calibration status, and defining the RF optimized
sequence.
Testflow variable RDI_CONFIGURE_FILE
This testflow variable allows you to select a customized RDI_Configure file for a testflow.
Therefore, you can have different setups in different RDI_Configure files for different
testflows.
Use this variable to specify a RDI_Configure file for a testflow each time. You can specify
as many RDI_Configure files to testflows as required. You can put your customized
RDI_Configure files to an absolute path or paths.
Keyword groups in the RDI_Configure file
Alarm handling for DCVI
Default pin status
For debugging
For production
MS-DPS HW trigger setup
Offline Result Emulation (ORE) setup
Pass or fail per label
PMUX setup
PPMU setup
Result upload
RF setup

Setup naming
smartVec setup
